The goal of the BCAT investigations is to further investigate critical, fundamental problems in colloid science and evolve the field of ‘colloid engineering’, which creates materials with novel properties using colloidal particles as precursors. The BCAT-4 investigation had two primary objectives corresponding to specific samples: Critical Point (BCAT-3-4-CP): Depending on their relative distances and energies with respect one another, atoms and molecules organize themselves to form gases, liquids, or solids. By varying the concentrations of the microscale spheres, this experiment studied the critical point of these systems where gases and liquids no longer exist as separate entities and a new state of matter forms when one reaches a critical point. Polydispersion (BCAT-4-Poly): BCAT-4-Poly will use model hard-spheres (suspended in a liquid that makes them transparent) to explore pure and seeded colloidal crystal nucleation and the effects of polydispersity, providing insight into how to understand and control the processes used by nature to bring order out of disorder.

Colloidal particles would exhibit behaviors analogous to atoms, allowing the study of phase transitions, crystallization, and self-organization without the interference of sedimentation and convection present on Earth. This investigation hypothesizes that by taking advantage of microgravity and avoiding sedimentation binary alloys with very different materials and sizes and by addition of polymers particles to induce attractive forces can lead to exciting and promising form of colloidal engineering to synthesize a new class of materials.

BCAT is implemented in a bench-top investigation which is set up on the Maintanence Work Area (MWA) on ISS. The first set of samples was composed of mixtures of colloids and polymers near their liquid-gas critical point. The second set consisted of spherical colloidal particles with effective volume fractions resulting in an amorphous or glassy phase in normal gravity. The samples are contained within a Fluids Module (FM) which held 10 samples in couvettes in individual wells. The samples were manually homogenized using a stirbar (a teflon coated mixing magnet) inside each couvette. Samples are mixed, examined and imaged using a digital EarthKAM camera to document the separation of colloid and liquid components and the formation of colloidal crystals over time.

The findings of BCAT-4 can directly contribute to the development of advanced materials for use in space missions, such as lightweight and durable composites for spacecraft or self-assembling structures for space habitats. Additionally, understanding colloidal behavior aids in the optimization of life support systems, such as those used for water recycling and air purification, which are vital for sustaining long-duration missions to destinations like Mars. On Earth, the results of BCAT-4 have practical applications across multiple industries, including consumer goods, medicine, and manufacturing. For instance, the study of colloidal stability and crystallization informs the design of more stable food products, cosmetics, and pharmaceutical formulations. The findings also enhance industrial processes like 3D printing, where precise control of particle interactions is crucial for producing high-quality materials. Furthermore, BCAT-4 contributes to advancements in medicine by improving drug delivery systems that rely on colloidal suspensions, ensuring more effective treatments. The primary objective of this research was to develop a numerical 3D model capable of simulating the pore-mushy zone interaction during directional solidification of Succinonitrile -Water alloys in microgravity and test the simulation results against the Pore Formation and Mobility Investigation (PFMI) microstructural observations, quantitatively and qualitatively.

Previous real time observations in transparent analogues of interactions between a bubble and an array of primary dendrites are essentially “two-dimensional” (2D) and are affected by the “wall” effects. Contrary to earlier belief, it is now recognized that the basic premise of such experiments, i.e. 2D dendrites represent morphology of a three-dimensional (3D) array, is false. This investigation hypothesizes that understanding pore-mushy zone interaction in real castings requires both the experimental observations and also the theoretical/numerical modeling with 3D array of dendrites.

This investigation exploited forefront methods in microscale solidification and developed models based on phase filed (PF), cellular automaton (CA) and Lattice Boltzmann (LB) to simulate pore formation and its motion during directional solidification. The results from the Pore Formation and Mobility Investigation (PFMI) experiments were conducted in the microgravity environment aboard the Space Station with the intent of better understanding the role entrained porosity/bubbles play on microstructure during controlled directional solidification (DS). Several sets of time-temperature-interface-bubble interaction data were extracted and analyzed from the PFMI videos. The simulation results were tested against the PFMI microstructural observations.

This investigation helped to explain fundamental aspects of the mechanisms that regulate the formation of microporosities. The formation of these defects depends on microstructure features that cannot be properly captured by current meso- and macro-scale models based on averaging techniques. The direct numerical simulation of bubble dynamics in a dendritic network can provide a relation between macroscopically observable variables like cooling rate or temperature gradient and difficult to measure dynamic microscopic features like microporosity distribution, interdendritic permeability, solute redistribution, and dendrite arm spacing. Keywords: PBRE · Packed Bed Reactor Experiment · PBRE-WR

The objective of the flight experiment was to study the hydrodynamics of packed beds in microgravity and under different gas and liquid flow conditions. The hydrodynamics consists of the pressure drop inside the packed bed and the liquid hold-up. The different regimes are the results of different liquid and gas flow rates, and different initial conditions embodied by gas and liquid pre-flow or flushes prior to beginning of the runs. Another objective of the experiment was to understand transient flow rates and the hysteresis in the pressure drop as a function of the flow rates.

While the overarching principles of two-phase flow in porous media apply, the specific material properties of alumina will cause unique flow phenomena, and models can be modified to account for such. Furthermore, this unique data is specifically relevant to the design and operation of reactors used in space-based water recovery systems, and the data can be used to improve and optimize such systems.

The PBRE-WR investigations employed a systematic and comprehensive approach to study the hydrodynamics of two-phase flow in packed bed reactors under microgravity conditions. The approach can be summarized in the following key steps:

1. Ground-Based Research and Model Development: Prior to the spaceflight experiments, extensive ground-based research was conducted to develop theoretical models and establish a foundation for understanding two-phase flow in packed beds. This included: Literature review: A thorough review of existing literature on single-phase and two-phase flow through porous media, focusing on pressure drop, flow regimes, and the influence of various parameters. Development of hydrodynamic models: Formulation of mathematical models, such as the modified Ergun equation, to predict pressure drop and flow regime transitions in microgravity. Ground-based experiments: Conducting experiments in reduced gravity environments, such as parabolic flights and drop towers, to gather preliminary data and validate initial model predictions.

2. Design and Development of Spaceflight Experiment: A dedicated experimental facility was designed and developed for operation on the ISS. This involved: Test facility design: Engineering a flow control system, test section, and data acquisition system capable of operating reliably in microgravity and meeting the specific requirements of the investigation. Selection of packing materials: PBRE-WR used 3.5 mm Alumina packing, a common inert material used in reactor beds such as water purification systems. Definition of test matrix: Developing a comprehensive test matrix encompassing a wide range of gas and liquid flow rates, pre-flow conditions, and transient flow scenarios.

3. Execution of Spaceflight Experiments: The PBRE-WR experiments were conducted on the ISS, following the defined test matrix and procedures. This involved: Preflow procedures: Implementing the chosen pre-flow treatment (liquid flush or gas flush) before each test run. Flow control: Precisely controlling and varying the gas and liquid flow rates according to the test matrix. Data acquisition: Collecting data from pressure sensors, temperature sensors, and high-speed cameras throughout each test run. Downlinking data: Transmitting the acquired data to the ground for analysis.

4. Data Analysis and Interpretation: The downlinked data was meticulously analyzed to: Characterize flow regimes: Identify and classify the different flow regimes observed in the experiments based on pressure traces and video recordings. Evaluate pressure drop: Analyze the pressure drop data and compare it with model predictions to assess the validity and accuracy of the models. Investigate flow regime transitions: Determine the conditions and mechanisms leading to transitions between different flow regimes. Assess the influence of packing properties and pre-flow conditions: Analyze the impact of packing material wettability, size, and pre-flow treatments on the flow behavior and pressure drop.
5. Dissemination of Results: The findings of the PBRE-WR investigations have not been completed and disseminated yet.

Fundamental understanding the impact of reduced or zero gravity on the hydrodynamics (pressure drop, as well as distribution and holdup of each phase) is relevant to systems that involve two-phase flow such as life support systems, fuel cells, in-situ resource utilization, heat pipes, materials processing, production of pharmaceutical-grade water, and transport of nutrients in soils. Design and operation of many chemical and biological processing systems require this fundamental understanding of two-phase gas-liquid flows through porous media because many of these space-based systems or unit operations involve gas-liquid flows through porous media. Some examples of current space systems involving two-phase flow through fixed porous media include the Volatile Removal Assembly (VRA), the Integrated Advanced Water Recovery System (AWRS), and IntraVenous Water GENeration system (IVGEN). The ability to predict flow regimes and corresponding pressure drop in a particular system involving two-phase flow is crucial to the design of the fluid system and the pumping requirements.

The ACE-M1 investigation aims to study the behavior of microscopic particles in colloidal mixtures such as gels and creams. Objectives include the study of the physics of colloidal coarsening and the role of polydispersity (variation in particle size) in determining the stability of colloidal systems. Previous Earth-based experiments show that polydispersity dramatically affects the time it takes for these gels to collapse. The imaging goal was to observe crystallites and resolve particle centroid positions with less than 20% error.

Polydispersity significantly affects the time scale and dynamics of coarsening. It is believed that polydispersity can lead to a substantial difference in the collapse time of weak gels, and understanding this effect in a microgravity environment can provide critical insights into product design and stability.

The ACE-M1 investigation utilized a Sample Cartridge disk with 10 Sample Wells for 10 samples. Samples were colloidal fluids of small and large particles in varying concentration over .5 to 2.0 mg/ml. Protocols included Homogenization and microscopic Observation and Imaging. A crew member used magnetic stir bars embedded in the sample well to homogenized each sample. Fluorescent microscopy and Imaging of the colloidal crystallites in each well as they developed over time allowed observation of particle movements and interactions to characterize and quantify rates of growth of structures formed.

Space Benefits: By conducting colloidal research in microgravity, the ACE-M1 experiment can obtain clearer data on the dynamics of liquid mixtures, free from the effects of gravitational forces. This research can improve the manufacturing processes for creating new, longer-lasting products for use both in space and on Earth. Earth Benefits: Understanding the behavior of colloidal mixtures and the coarsening process can help materials scientists design products with longer shelf lives. This has significant implications for a wide range of products, including food, medicine, cosmetics, gels, and cleaning solutions, potentially leading to reduced waste and enhanced product performance​.

The ACE-T7 experiment involves the design and assembly of complex 3D structures from small particles suspended within a fluid medium. These so-called “self-assembled colloidal structures”, are vital to the design of advanced optical materials and active devices. The objective of ACE-T7 was to utilize confocal microscopy for time- and space-resolved, 3D imaging of non-spherical colloids whose phases can be controlled by adding depletants and/or adjusting spatial temperature changes around a particular location. The research goal is to produce cubic colloidal structures, and study the dynamics of crystal nucleation and growth. ACE-T7 varied the size of the depletant in different samples with the goal of seeing the effect on crystallization. The imaging goal was to observe crystallites and resolve particle centroid positions with less than 20% error.

It is hypothesized that under certain conditions, the particles should self-organize into crystals with simple cubic symmetry, which is set by the size of the nano-size depletant. Increasing particle number density using a temperature gradient, i.e., thermophoresis, is expected to induce formation of crystallites. Three-dimensional structures that are impossible to create or reform on earth due to sedimentation issues (high density contrast between particles and fluid) should be observed in microgravity.

The ACE-T7 experiment used the Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) and the Light Microscopy Module (LMM) with enhancements. ACE-T7 utilized two sample cartridges, each having three temperature-controlled capillaries for a total of six samples; each capillary volume has 50 mm length, 2.0 mm ID width, and 0.2 mm ID height, with automated mixing capabilities using magnetic stir bars embedded in the capillaries. Each sample volume was about 20 μl. Each cartridge could be heated or cooled uniformly via Peltier temperature control. In total, six capillaries are prepared, numbered C1-C6. The three primary science objectives are to measure the initial on-orbit thermal performance, to measure long duration thermal performance, and to assess any lifetime degradation. Flight data will be used to validate microgravity portions of an OHP operating limits model recently published by members of the team. Returned flight experiment hardware will be subjected to post-flight testing to assess the presence of any non-condensable gas that may have formed on orbit.
Oscillating heat pipes will exhibit consistent and stable thermal performance in a long-duration microgravity environment, comparable to their performance in a terrestrial setting.

The ASETS-II experiment is made of three low-mass, low-cost OHPs and an electronics experiment control box. The three OHPs are of varying configuration (center heating with single- and double-sided cooling) and working fluids (butane and R-134a) in order to isolate specific performance parameters of interest. In addition to serving as a science experiment, the ASETS-II flight experiment serves as a pathfinder for incorporating high performance OHP-based thermal spreaders into flat plate structures such as electronics chip carriers, thermal ground planes, and spacecraft panels. Microgravity influence on fluid flow, especially two-phase flow, is significantly different than in a terrestrial environment. This is true for steady-state operations, but is more important for transient operation. In addition, the combined effects of the space environment (e.g. thermal Cutaway of an oscillating heat pipe (OHP) showing its microchannel pattern cycling, high vacuum, charging, vibration) are required to verify the performance of the system on orbit for long durations.

Potentially shift the way NASA designs its future deep space craft and extraterrestrial human habitats, providing safer, more reliable temperature regulation for the human occupants and the sensitive technology housed inside Cooling electronics.

InSPACE-3 investigated the assembly of paramagnetic colloidal ellipsoids in pulsed magnetic fields. An objective was to study the effect of particle shape on the kinetics of aggregation and structures formed by DC and pulsed magnetic fields in suspensions of superparamagnetic particles. Specifically, the investigation studied the suspensions of paramagnetic ellipsoid-shaped particles and quantify the effect of particle shape on the interactions of dipolar chains and the resulting suspension microstructure.

Based on the science results of InSPACE-2, InSPACE-3 hypothesizes that particle shape will alter the aggregation kinetics, microstructures and microscopic mechanics, such as buckling instabilities that are observed for suspensions of polarizable spheres. This research will potentially lead to the ability to engineer enhanced properties of these suspensions, including the ability to suppress lateral aggregation in magnetorheological fluid-based electromechanical devices or the ability to create new functional materials that control the flow of electromagnetic and thermal energy.

InSPACE-3 employed video microscopy to obtain suspension structural information. Two particle shapes were tested for four frequency conditions and four field strengths, for a total of 24 experimental runs. Each run took approximately one hour. Each sample had a particle volume fraction of 0.52%. This concentration represents an optimum value based on previous microgravity experiments, designed to balance the ability to capture aggregation kinetics at short times in DC fields the structural evolution in pulsed fields such that the final coalescence stage is observed. For detailed experimental approach please refer Science Requirements Document (SRD).

The quick phase-shifting property of magnetic colloidal fluids studied in InSPACE-3 makes them potentially useful for devices such as optical interfaces, active noise, and vibration dampers inside spacecrafts. Future uses could include robotics, energy-transfer devices such as clutches, and other control systems and on Earth directed self-assembly of crystalline structures from particles that may eventually allow creation of new nano-materials fabricated from nanoparticle building blocks, with potential applications in medicine, energy storage, chemical separations, and catalysis. Magnetic colloidal fluid technology is currently used for shock absorbers in race cars and sport cars. This technology is expanding to include making large-scale building foundation stabilizers for areas prone to earthquakes.

The Consortium’s work is described in the context of four Tasks. Task 1: Advanced Clocks in Space and Time Transfer Task 2: Maturing and Advancing Atom Interferometer Technology for Space Task 3: Precision Atom Interferometric Measurement in Space Task 4: Strategies for the Frontier of Ultracold Atoms in Space.

The Consortium is: N. P. Bigelow, M. Kasevick, W. Ketterle, M. Lukin, H. Müller, W. D. Phillips, D. Pritchard, D. Stamper-Kurn, V. Vuletic, and J. Ye. Berkeley and Stanford lead Tasks 2 and 3. MIT, U.C./JILA, and Harvard lead Task 1. U. Md., Rochester, and MIT lead Task 4. Members of the Consortium can and often will contribute to all four tasks with priorities being set by the lead institutions.

This consortium aims to provide a space for the world’s experts on Bose-Einstein Condensates (BEC), atom optics, atom interferometry, and related quantum realms to push the current boundaries of quantum gas and atomic physics space experiments. It is hypothesized that with the realization of a space atom laser and precision atomic interferometry there is potential for significant scientific advancement by testing the equivalence principle with quantum test masses and pushing the limits of the standard model. A space atom laser is expected to provide truly novel investigations of the wave-like nature of matter. Varied experiments and manipulation of quantum gases (both single-species and dual-species) including deep cooling, condensate mixture phases, and precision motional control are hypothesized to mature the technology of quantum gases and provide first of its kind opportunity to investigate interacting quantum gases in space.

The Consortium for Ultracold Atoms in Space (CUAS), led by Nicholas Bigelow, conducted groundbreaking experiments in atomic clocks, atom interferometry, and quantum gases, with a strong focus on the application of these quantum technologies in space environments. The consortium's research was guided by the objectives outlined in the National Research Council (NRC) report and NASA's Research Announcement (NRA), particularly in precision measurement and quantum gas studies. The Consortium fostered a collaborative approach, bringing together scientists from top institutions like MIT, Stanford, Berkeley, and Harvard, as well as international partners such as those from the DLR (German Space Agency). This collaboration allowed the group to pool expertise, regularly refine their goals, and push forward only the most promising space experiments.

The procedure for the creation of an ultracold gas is fairly standardized. The atoms are released into a vacuum chamber, collected into a magneto-optical trap (MOT), and cooled via laser cooling. The sample is then optically pumped to a low magnetic field seeking quantum state and transfer from the MOT to an atom-chip based trap. The atoms are then evaporatively cooled to below the critical temperature so that a Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC) begins to form. The atom trap is slightly relaxed to further cool the atoms, and eventually the atoms are completely released from the trap and allowed to expand freely. At this point, the ultracold gas is probed using laser, radiofrequency, and/or microwave pulses. After a prespecified time of flight, the sample is imaged using absorption imaging techniques. This is the end of the experimental cycle for this specific BEC because the measurement process destroys the sample. A total of two images are taken, the first being an image of the sample and the second being a reference image that is taken after the destructive absorption imaging process. This general process was followed by the Consortium for experiments requiring the production or pro

In their work on atom interferometry, the Consortium conducted experiments to detect dark-energy scalar fields with unprecedented sensitivity. The team also focused on measuring the fine structure constant with high accuracy, which involved overcoming systematic effects that could be amplified in the space environment. Collaborations with the Bose-Einstein Condensate and Cold Atom Laboratory (BECCAL) science definition team and other international partners were essential for demonstrating long coherence times in microgravity, testing the equivalence principle, and searching for dark-energy candidates. These experiments were conducted with a focus on utilizing the microgravity conditions available aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and other space-based platforms, which provided a unique environment to achieve results unattainable on Earth.

In the realm of atomic clocks and quantum sensors, the Consortium developed new configurations for optical lattice clocks and achieved precision at the 19th decimal place, setting a new record for stable laser performance with a linewidth of 10 mHz. These experiments were designed to improve the accuracy of space-based timekeeping and navigation systems, which are critical for the success of space missions. The Consortium also explored innovative cooling methods, such as direct optical cooling to achieve Bose-Einstein condensation, which simplified the setup for quantum experiments in space. These methods were tested and refined in microgravity environments, demonstrating their potential to enhance the performance of quantum technologies in space.

Overall, the Consortium’s approach to conducting experiments was characterized by a strong emphasis on leveraging the unique conditions of space, particularly microgravity, to achieve results that would be impossible on Earth. Their collaborative efforts, cutting-edge experimental designs, and focus on precision allowed them to make significant contributions to the field of quantum technologies in space, laying the groundwork for future space missions and advancing our understanding of fundamental physics.

Significant progress has been made on atomic interferometry and atomic clocks in terrestrial experiments. The work has long-term impact for fundamental science, navigation technologies, and global clock synchronization. Clocks are vital to navigation, communication, and security.

ATOM INTERFEROMETRY We have pushed atom interferometry for space applications forward in many ways: 1. We have shown that atom interferometry can detect dark-energy scalar fields with unprecedented sensitivity. There is a chance to cover all the relevant parameter space so as to detect them or to rule them out once and for all. This work has been published in Science, Nature Physics, and Physical Review D. 2. Development of Atom Interferometry Experiments for the International Space Station's Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL- Atom Interferometry) demonstrates using atom interferometry as a precision measurement technique on the space station. Atom interferometry is an ultra-sensitive measurement technique that splits the quantum wave function of an atom into two distinct wave packets that travel separate trajectories and then recombine. This technique, already demonstrated on the ground, should work better in space and could be useful for future space navigation systems.

This investigation hypothesizes that, combined with the current atomic cooling techniques, the implementation of expansion cooling will produce atoms with temperatures on the order of a trillionth of a degree above absolute zero (10^-12 K). With the unique settings provided by Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL) the maximum expansion and low temperature limits are able to be probed. Atomic interferometry can be used to measure the acceleration of cold atoms relative to the International Space Station, allowing investigators to explore using ultracold atoms as part of an inertial navigation system.

This investigation uses rubidium (87Rb) and potassium (39K and 41K) samples in the Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL) aboard the International Space Station (ISS). The approach for the flight-based investigation comprises two main aspects: the creation of ultracold atomic gases and the subsequent manipulation and probing of these gases to study systematic mitigations. For dual-species operations the process is slightly more complicated, especially with the addition of a sympathetic cooling step, however, the general process is fairly standardized. 1. Creation of Ultracold Atomic Gas: • Laser Cooling: Atoms are released into a vacuum chamber and collected into a magneto-optical trap (MOT), where they are initially cooled using laser cooling techniques. This technique cools the sample by essentially ‘pushing’ the laser against the motion of the atoms effectively lowering the momentum, and therefore the velocity, kinetic energy, and temperature, of the sample. This is followed by a brief stage of “optical molasses” during which the quadrupole magnetic field is turned off and the laser frequency is further detuned. • State Preparation: The sample is optically pumped to a low magnetic field-see

This approach is particularly suited for studying mitigation schemes for leading-order systematics that can affect future high-precision measurements with atom interferometers (AIs) in microgravity. This investigation utilizes the atom interferometry equipment aboard the CAL instrument for precision measurement experiments. The BEC formed according to the steps laid out in the Creation of Ultracold Atomic Gases section is split using an off resonance standing wave laser. The split waves packets will travel different trajectories, and then recombine after a secondary laser beam is applied. After the recombination, the atomic interference pattern can be collected. The flight-based results can be compared to theoretical investigations and ground studies done at JPL, enabling comprehensive understanding and development of systematic mitigation techniques.

The development of precision inertial sensing techniques is useful for Earth-based as well as space-based navigation. Besides using direct sensing for inertial navigation, rotation sensing can also be useful for north-finding while gravity sensing can be used to tabulate local gravity variations and form a type of three-dimensional map for navigating.

These techniques also have many applications in geophysics. Gravity sensing can be used for oil and mineral exploration, while rotation sensing can detect dynamics in the Earth's core. Gravity sensing also has defense applications such as locating underground tunnels and potential screening cargo for high-density contraband or weapons.

Other precision measurement applications have less direct impact, but advance scientific knowledge. For instance, precision tune-out spectroscopy measurements of atomic matrix elements can be used to improve the interpretation of atomic parity violation experiments. These in turn impact our understanding of the standard model of particle physics and thus the nature of our universe. Direct benefits of such understanding can be hard to trace, but in general the continued advance of technological applications builds on advances in our fundamental knowledge.

The objective of the CSLM-2R investigation was essentially the same as the original CSLM investigation with the focus on lower solid volume percent samples.

The theory of coarsening has been described by Lifshitz, Slyozov and Wagner (LSW) predicts that for the limit of zero volume fraction particles grow with time as the cube root of the average radius, and the particle size distribution becomes independent of time. The investigation hypothesizes that finding a system which satisfies all the constraints of LSW theory such as particles are infinitely separated and there is no diffusional interaction between them is prohibitive for ground-based laboratory condition due to effects of particle sedimentation and buoyancy-induced convection and therefore the theory can only be tested by performing experiments in a microgravity environment.

The CSLM-2R approach and hardware was identical to the predecessor CSLM-2 investigation. The solid volume fraction of the 4 samples for CSLM-2R were 0.05. 0.10, 0.15, and 0.20 and the coarsening times ranged from 1.6 to 48 hours.

Coarsening occurs on Earth during the processing of any metal alloy and thus the coarsening process affects a large spectrum of products from dental fillings to turbine blades. Since the properties of an alloy are linked to the size of the particles within the solid, coarsening can be used to strengthen materials. This is the case with the majority of aluminum alloys used commercially today. Conversely, if the coarsening process proceeds too long the material can weaken. This occurs in jet turbine blades and is one of the reasons why turbine blades must be replaced after a certain number of hours of service. Thus developing accurate models of the coarsening process is central to creating a wide range of new materials encompassing those used in automobiles to those used in space applications.

Zero-G Studies of Few-Body and Many-Body Physics (Cold Atom Lab - Few-Body Physics) investigates the dynamics of interacting ultracold atoms under varying conditions. The dynamics of few-body systems comprised of just three or four atoms can strongly influence the collective behavior of quantum gases and play an important role in development of quantum gas applications. Modern laser cooling techniques are used to chill atoms to near absolute zero temperatures. At these temperatures, atoms behave like matter waves, according to the laws of quantum mechanics. Fully automated data runs, each lasting about one minute, acquire images of ultracold atom clouds under varying conditions. The acquired data fills a critical need for the development of detailed and precise atomic physics models. The development of these models is performed in theoretical studies accompanying the data gathering campaigns with the CAL instrument. Studying the behavior and interaction of few atoms in microgravity could provide important data for developing a precise theory describing quantum gases on a microscopic level. The knowledge gained in this study also aids in the development of future quantum technologie

Ultracold atoms in microgravity provide a unique environment for the study of complex few-body phenomena. One of the surprising predictions for quantum mechanical few-body systems is the existence of universality, i.e. the idea that highly intricate phenomena can be governed by underlying principles that are agnostic to specific microscopic realizations. As a concrete example, Efimov physics predicts the emergence of an infinite series of exotic three-body bound states when the interactions between the atoms are made stronger and stronger. It is predicted that these Efimov states are connected by universal scaling relations governing their energy and their size. Our experiments aim to provide essential benchmark data to test this universality hypothesis. By measuring two members of this infinite series, scaling relations can be probed and can be compared to some of the most advanced few-body theories to date. This will be a steppingstone towards the investigation of a plethora of associated few-body phenomena, with the ultimate goal of significantly advancing the boundary of our understanding and paving the way for the development of new quantum technologies.

The Zero-G Studies of Few-Body and Many-Body Physics investigation uses rubidium (87Rb) and potassium (39K and 41K) samples in the Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL) aboard the International Space Station (ISS). The approach for the investigation comprises two main aspects: the creation of ultracold atomic gases and the subsequent manipulation and probing of these gases to study few-body physics and exotic quantum states. Modern laser-cooling techniques are used to cool atoms to near absolute zero temperatures. At these temperatures, atoms behave like matter waves, according to the laws of quantum mechanics. Fully automated data runs, each lasting about one minute, acquire images of ultracold atom clouds under varying conditions.

1. Creation of Ultracold Atomic Gas: • Laser Cooling: Atoms are released into a vacuum chamber and collected into a magneto-optical trap (MOT), where they are initially cooled using laser cooling techniques. This technique is based on the rapid scattering of light off atoms and can cool a cloud of atoms to temperatures below 1x10-3 K. An additional magnetic field applied in conjunction with the lasers concentrates the cold atoms in a specific region of the vacuum apparatus, called the source chamber. The MOT is the starting point for further cooling and experimental preparation. • State Preparation: Using further laser manipulations, the atoms are then prepared in a state that seeks to occupy regions of low magnetic fields. By applying a suitable magnetic field geometry with a moving magnetic minimum, the cloud of atoms is transported to a so-called “science region.” Magnetic fields generated by a chip with current-carrying traces provide a trap for the atoms in the science region. • Evaporative Cooling: With the atoms trapped in the science region, evaporative cooling is performed by selectively removing the hottest rubidium atoms from the cloud. The remaining atoms then rethermal

2. Manipulation and Detection: • Manipulation Techniques: The ultracold gas is manipulated using laser, radiofrequency, and/or microwave pulses. In addition, homogeneous magnetic fields are used to shift internal energy levels of the atoms. These techniques are designed to adjust the pairwise interactions as needed for the preparation of exotic quantum states. • Time-of-Flight Imaging: After a predetermined time-of-flight during which the cloud is released from the trap and can expand freely, the sample is imaged using absorption imaging techniques. For this, a short laser pulse is flashed onto the atoms, and the shadow cast by the atoms is imaged on a CCD camera using a custom microscope setup. This imaging process typically destroys the “quantumness” of the sample and concludes an experimental cycle. The apparatus then starts over with the preparation of a new sample. Many cycles are performed during a typical data-taking campaign, with a time scale of approximately one minute per run.

Physics is the discipline that provides understanding of biology and chemistry at the most microscopic level, and the area within physics most relevant to chemistry and biology is “few-body physics.” It is an often neglected portion of physics, because it is so difficult to do. An important way to make progress is to simplify, simplify, simplify: to come up with model systems in which we can make progress that can later be applied to human-centric disciplines like biology, and develop exotic and useful new materials. A promising way to simplify is to study matter at lower temperature, and lower densities. The Cold-Atom Lab (CAL) flying in the International Space Station (ISS) is where we will reach the lowest possible temperatures, and low densities, to perform studies of simple, yet intricate (think “snowflakes”) clusters of three or four atoms.

Ultracold atomic gases are a key platform for a broad range of future quantum technologies, including ultraprecise sensing and timekeeping, novel medical imaging methods, secure communication schemes, high-performance computing, and development of exotic materials. A precise knowledge of few-body physics is necessary to fully realize the potential of quantum technologies. This project supports development of a detailed understanding of quantum mechanical few-body physics at the microscopic level, which may open new avenues for quantum gas applications in future space exploration. Such applications include inertial navigation and precision measurements using atom interferometry, or calibration standards for detectors used in astronomy.

The main objectives of the present work are to investigate: 1. The onset conditions and nature of oscillatory flows. 2. The effect of the heating mode and the static free surface shape on the oscillations. 3. The shape and motion of the free surface during oscillations. 4. The coupling among the free surface deformation, the surface temperature distribution, and the velocity field.

The onset of oscillatory thermocapillary flow, particularly in microgravity environments, is significantly influenced by free surface deformation, which acts in conjunction with the Marangoni number (Ma). • Buoyancy masks the true oscillation mechanism in Earth- based experiments: The experimental data on oscillatory thermocapillary flows taken in normal gravity environments are often confusing or contradictory due to the presence of buoyancy. This suggests that buoyancy may obscure the role of free surface deformation in the oscillation process. • Marangoni number alone is insufficient to predict oscillations in microgravity: The unexpected stability observed in the prior STDCE microgravity experiments, even at Marangoni numbers exceeding the critical threshold observed in ground-based tests, indicates that Ma is not the sole determinant of oscillatory onset in the absence of buoyancy. • Free surface deformation is a key factor: The interaction between thermocapillary forces and free surface deformation plays a key role in the oscillation mechanism.
The STDCE-2 investigation employed a systematic approach to explain the role of free surface deformation in oscillatory thermocapillary flows under microgravity conditions. This approach comprised:

Controlled Variation of Key Parameters: -Container Size: Utilizing three chamber diameters (1.2 cm, 2.0 cm, 3.0 cm) allowed researchers to examine the influence of scale on the onset of oscillations and assess potential inertial effects. -Heating Mode: Employing both submerged heater (CT mode) and CO2 laser (CF mode) systems enabled the comparison of flow behavior under constant temperature difference and constant heat flux boundary conditions, respectively. -Free Surface Shape: Tests were conducted with flat, concave, and convex free surfaces to explore the interplay between surface curvature and flow dynamics.

Advanced Diagnostic Techniques: -Flow Visualization: The use of tracer particles enabled the visualization and qualitative characterization of flow patterns, including the three-dimensional, time-dependent structures observed during oscillations. -Infrared Imaging: An infrared scanner captured the temperature distribution across the oil's free surface, providing insights into the thermal gradients driving the thermocapillary flow and their evolution during oscillations. -Optical Deformation Measurement: A Ronchi system was employed to measure the free surface deformation and motions, allowing researchers to quantify the dynamic changes in surface shape and correlate them with observed flow behavior and temperature variations.

Interactive Operation: The experiment was conducted interactively, allowing the researchers on the ground to communicate with the astronauts onboard the Spacelab, observe the downlinked video images in real-time, and adjust test parameters based on the observed phenomena. This flexibility facilitated the exploration of unexpected results and the fine-tuning of the experimental conditions to optimize data collection. The STDCE-2 investigation gathered comprehensive data aimed at complex dynamics of oscillatory thermocapillary flows and verifying the hypothesized role of free surface deformation in their onset.

Direct observation of pore/bubble formation and their mobility during processing in a microgravity environment will provide insight regarding the minimization of this detrimental feature during solidification processing of important metal alloys and semiconductors.

The PArticle STAbilised emulsions experiment (PASTA) is placed inside the Fluid Science Rack (FSL) in the European Columbus module of the ISS. Emulsions have large relevance for applications in a wide spectrum of technologies, processes, and products in different fields including oil and gas, specialty materials, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and foods. Both stable and unstable emulsions are needs that are shared across a variety of applications. For example, efficient de-emulsifiers are needed to facilitate the process of phase separation (breaking) in the crude oil emulsions extracted from the wells, while high stability oil-in-water emulsions are required in the final stage of production of the same well or to facilitate pumping high-viscosity oils through pipelines. In the food industry, many products based on emulsified fats or oils (condiments, sauces, frozen confections, and others) require long term stability. Some colloids (a system of fine particles suspended in a fluid) have the ability to act like a gas, liquid, solid, or even glass, depending on the relative concentration between the suspended material and the solution they are suspended in, and/or the presence or absence of gravity. The investigation aims to determine critical flow rates (choking) for wedge channels across various lengths and wedge angles. It explores choking behavior across capillary-inertial, visco-capillary, and overlap flow regimes. Bubble transport, migration, and phase separation within wedge geometries will also be investigated, focusing on the influence of flow rate, channel length, and bubble diameter.

The central hypothesis for CCF-CV EU2 is that a critical flow rate limit also exists in open capillary channels with wedge and gapped-wedge geometries, and it is governed by the interplay of capillary, viscous, and inertial forces. It is expected that the critical flow rate will be a function of the channel geometry, which includes the wedge angle and channel length, and that there will be different flow regimes which are linked to the governing flow forces. Furthermore, it is hypothesized that the nature of bubble transport, migration, and phase separation will depend on the flow conditions, such as flow rate and channel length, as well as bubble properties, such as the size and frequency.

The objective is to take advantage of microgravity to eliminate drainage and to use imaging and multiple light scattering diagnostics in order to non-invasively measure and elucidate the time evolution of key features of the bubble-packing structure of wet foams – namely, the bubble size distribution and bubble rearrangement dynamics – and how they are affected by degree of wetness by systematically increasing the liquid content for sequences of otherwise identical foams. Experiment Cells The FOAM-C experimental set-up comprises five segments with a total of 20 small test cells containing a variety of liquid mixtures. The Fluid Science Laboratory on the ISS Columbus module will automatically shake and analyze these mixtures using complex laser optics, highly sensitive photodiodes and high-resolution cameras that can take up to 10,000 images per second.
Each test cell weighs only 20 grams and contains less than 2 cm³ of the liquid mixture, while each segment comprises four test cells and weighs a total of 320 grams.

Another cell with a different composition (liquid fraction, concentration) is then subject of a new series of experiments.
Granular matter samples of defined volume concentration shall be agitated until a steady state is reached.
Consequently, optical diagnostics measure the grains dynamics in the steady state and after turning the agitation off.

The maximum experiment duration shall be assumed with 24h per experiment run for each sample. At the beginning of a science campaign on orbit replaceable units shall be exchanged (if necessary) and the EC is installed in FSL by the Crew. Each run starts with the foaming process. The Constrained Vapor Bubble (CVB) Experiment was conducted on the International Space Station (ISS) and the temperature data have been used to analyze the heat transfer mechanisms operating within the quartz cuvette for 40 mm and 30 mm modules. Even with the large millimeter dimensions of the CVB, interfacial forces dominate in these exceedingly small Bond Number systems with small viscous losses. The internal heat transfer processes were very complicated, multidimensional, and the length of the closed system strongly affected the average internal heat transfer processes. Most liquids have a surface tension that decreases as temperature rises. This causes fluid to flow in the direction of higher surface tension, a phenomenon known as Marangoni flow. This reduces the effectiveness of a heat pipe, because liquid cannot return to the hot end. CVB-2 investigates whether a mixture of two fuels (pentane and isohexane) that can reduce Marangoni flow and improve the efficiency of the CVB system on the International Space Station. In addition, the investigation provides insight into how heat transfer functions in microgravity. Most satellites use heat pipes to keep critical parts cool, and improved understanding of fluid mixtures could enable future heat pipes that are smaller, lighter and less expensive to launch. Sometimes its hard to tell a gas from a liquid. ACE-M2R observes the microscopic behavior of liquids and gases separating from each other. The investigation examines the behavior of model (colloid rich) liquids and model (colloid poor) gases near the critical point, or the point at which there is no distinct boundary between the two phases. ACE-M2R uses a new microscope to record micro-scale events on short time scales, while previous experiments observed large-scale behavior over many weeks. Liquids and gases of the same material usually have different densities, so they would behave differently under the influence of gravity, making the microgravity environment of the International Space Station ideal for these experiments.
This investigation is a re-flight of the original ACE-M2 with the intent to resolve issues from the original flight.

Near the critical point, variations in density and effective temperature will significantly influence particle interactions, leading to observable changes in phase stability and transition behavior. These changes are expected to reveal underlying mechanisms governing critical phenomena in colloidal systems, enhancing the predictability of particle dynamics in similar environments.

The ACE-M2 investigation utilized 2 Sample Modules (1 is duplicate for back-up) with 15 Sample Wells each for a total of 30 samples, 15 flight and 15 slight identical for back-up. Samples were colloidal fluids varying concentrations of two different types of fluorescent dye and particle size; large and small. Magnetic stir bars embedded in each sample well were used to homogenized each sample. Fluorescent microscopy and Imaging of the colloidal crystallites in each well as they developed over time allowed observation of particle movements and interactions to characterize and quantify rates of growth of structures formed.

Space Applications: On Earth, gravity plays a big role in how liquids and gases interact: The heavier liquid phase settles beneath a lighter gas phase, and these differences in density enable easy separation. But the flow and behavior of complex fluids and phase separation where there is little or no gravity is not well understood. A greater understanding of liquid-gas interaction in microgravity could benefit a wide range of fluid storage, transport and processing systems for future spacecraft. Earth Applications: Particle separation and behavior in liquids, gels, and creams is important for developing consumer and household products, which are worth billions of dollars annually to the U.S. economy. Many consumer products are complex fluids, combining microscopic particles in gel or liquid, which are similar to the model colloidal system used in the ACE investigations which give insight into product formulations that could be used to maximize stability and shelf life.

passages: PSI-77 · ISSI — In Space Soldering Investigation

Keywords: In-Space Soldering · Microgravity · surface tension gradient · Welding · porosity · kinematic and dynamic viscosity

The primary objective is to better understand the quality of solders in a microgravity environment. In microgravity, gas bubbles, or void spaces are found in the solder joint and at contact surfaces. These voids reduce the thermal and electrical conductivity and also provide sites for crack initiation. Bubbles have less chance to escape in the reduced gravity environment of space. Hence, by designing a systematic series of simple experiments, the objective was to investigate and better understand porosity development, surface wetting, and equilibrium shape formation while soldering in a reduced gravity environment.

Due to minimized buoyancy in the microgravity environment, it is hypothesized that one would expect additional porosity and enhanced surface tension contributions to porosity shape and mobility. Brazing, soldering, and welding operations in microgravity can be influenced greatly by both wetting and surface tension-driven flows, primary factors in achieving or not achieving a sound joint. For example, processes that rely on gravity-driven separations in the terrestrial environment, such as the removal of gas bubbles from a liquid, may rely on completely different interfacial phenomenon in microgravity.

The proposed experiments basically consisted of taking pieces of silver-coated copper wire and bending/twisting them into simple configurations for test coupons. Selected lengths of Kester “44”® 60-40 rosin core solder (5 and 10 cm) were then cut and wrapped around a selected portion of the coupon, to be later melted by heat conduction through the wire using the kit’s soldering iron. A second set of experiments involved feeding 5 and 10 cm lengths of solder onto similar shaped coupons that were being heated by the iron. In principle, the soldering iron was never meant to come in contact with the molten solder. All in all, five soldering sessions were conducted on the ISS that culminated in 86 samples comprising seven different wire configurations, two different solder lengths (5 and 10 cm), and two different melt procedures (conduction melting of wrapped solder and conduction melting of solder being fed onto the wire). The melting experiments took place in the flame retardant Maintenance Work Area, a portable facility in the ISS used to make repairs and conduct other operations in the ISS. A digital camera is placed behind the samples to record the melting and subsequent solidifica

An investigation of soldering practices and behavior in a microgravity environment is relevant to our technological needs, particularly with regard to in-space fabrication and repair. The ISSI payload provides unique insight into microgravity soldering methods, which could play a fundamental role in maintaining the International Space Station as well as provide understanding of repair capabilities on future missions to the Moon and to Mars. The study of soldering in space could lead to better soldering techniques here on Earth.

Keywords: Colloid · crystallization · rheology · Self-assembly · 3D structures · Hard Spheres · temperature gradient

ACE-T11 studies the design and assembly of complex 3D structures from small particles suspended within a fluid medium with control of particle density, phase and behavior. Objectives included study of nucleation and growth of crystals within colloidal samples by varying the size and concentration of colloids and depletant, exploring the effect of temperature gradients, and demonstrating control of particle shape and density which is essential for creating high performance materials for 3D printing and advanced optical materials. The research goal is to produce various colloidal structures and study the dynamics of crystal nucleation and growth. The imaging goal is to observe crystallites and resolve particle centroid positions with less than 20% error.

Under microgravity conditions, colloidal particles would exhibit unique crystallization and self-assembly behaviors that differ from those observed under Earth's gravity. Researchers believed that without the effects of sedimentation, they would better understand the fundamental mechanisms governing colloidal phase transitions and self-organization​. This hypothesis also included the idea that controlling external factors like temperature and depletant concentration would enable precise manipulation of colloidal structures, allowing for the creation of more complex and functional materials.

The ACE-T11 investigation used 2 Sample Modules (SM), each containing 3 capillary cells for a total of 6 samples. Confocal microscopy was employed for 3D imaging of non-spherical colloids, with phases controlled by adding depletants, adjusting spatial temperature changes, and applying temperature gradients. The size and concentration of both the particles and depletants were varied across different samples. After homogenization using a magnetic stirrer, the particles were left undisturbed to crystallize. Preliminary observations were made with a 2.5X objective, followed by detailed imaging using 10X, 63X, and 100X objectives.

Future space missions will require self-assembly and self-replication technologies for self-repairing materials and devices, essential for long-duration travel. 3D printing and additive manufacturing are crucial for creating replacement parts, with research focusing on developing particle slurries and pastes suited for both micro and regular gravity environments. This research advances soft matter science, with applications in medicine, electronics, and photonics. Self-assembly techniques will enable new devices for energy and communication, while 3D printing and additive manufacturing rely on optimizing high-density slurries and pastes with diverse mechanical properties.

SHERE-II investigation involves a non-Newtonian fluid that will undergo preshearing (rotation) for a specified period of time, followed by stretching. This combination of shearing and extensional deformations is common in many earth-based polymer processing and manufacturing operations such as extrusion, blow-molding and fiber spinning. However, in order to accurately predict the flow behaviour of polymeric fluids under such deformation histories, an accurate knowledge of the extensional viscosity of a polymer system and its variation with strain rate is critical and will be measured during this experiment. The fundamental understanding and measurement of these complex fluids is important for containerless processing, a key operation for fabrication of parts, such as adhesives or fillers, using elastomeric materials on future exploration missions.

SHERE-II is designed to investigate the effects of a pre-shear history on the transient extensional viscosity in a uniaxial stretching flow for a model filled viscoelastic suspension (consisting of inert rigid non-Brownian spheres dispersed in a dilute polymer solution).This experiment will generate additional scientific data for dilute viscoelastic polymer solutions in a broad subclass of transient uniaxial extensional flows.Understanding extensional rheology is key in understanding how to process thermoplastic elastomers (flexible elastic polymeric materials), which are very resilient and can be made very thin, and hence, lightweight.Understanding the rheological properties of highly viscoelastic suspensions may be of paramount importance for lunar in-situ resource utilization and for the future construction of a permanent lunar base.SHERE can provide data for engineering design tools that are part of computer-assisted manufacturing (CAM) systems to ensure that the rheological properties of polymeric parts have not been impacted in a variable gravity environment

Understanding the extensional rheology of a complex fluid such as a liquid polymer is key for containerless processing because the absence of the bounding walls of a container or vessel removes the shearing component of the deformation which typically dominates earth-based processing operations. The resulting flow is thus shear-free or extensional in character. Containerless processing is a central component in the development of in-situ fabrication technology, such as a means of producing new parts on demand or replacing existing parts or tools. This represents a critical element in the evolution of an autonomous exploration capability. In-situ fabricated parts, which may include both new and recycled materials, will be composed of plastics, filled polymers, metals, ceramics and composites. SHERE plays a role in SHERE plays a role in this area by measuring, in microgravity conditions, a material property that has a direct connection to in-situ manufacturing and fabrication of polymeric parts. In-situ manufacturing operations can occur in microgravity or reduced gravity levels (e.g. on the Moon or Mars) and may include for example, the extrusion and processing of thermoplastic elas

The objective of the CSLM-2 investigation was essentially the same as the original CSLM investigation with the addition of higher solid volume percent samples requiring longer times to reach steady state coarsening rates.

The theory of coarsening has been described by Lifshitz, Slyozov and Wagner (LSW) predicts that for the limit of zero volume fraction particles grow with time as the cube root of the average radius, and the particle size distribution becomes independent of time. The investigation hypothesizes that finding a system which satisfies all the constraints of LSW theory such as particles are infinitely separated and there is no diffusional interaction between them is prohibitive for ground-based laboratory condition due to effects of particle sedimentation and buoyancy-induced convection and therefore the theory can only be tested by performing experiments in a microgravity environment, For CSLM-2 it is hypothesized that for large volume fraction solid samples the transient coarsening process will be longer and steady state will be reached much later compared to low volume fraction solid particles.
The CSLM-2 approach and hardware was identical to the predecessor CSLM investigation. The solid volume fraction of the 4 samples for CSLM-2 were 0.3. 0.5, 0.7, and 0.8.

Coarsening occurs on Earth during the processing of any metal alloy and thus the coarsening process affects a large spectrum of products from dental fillings to turbine blades. Since the properties of an alloy are linked to the size of the particles within the solid, coarsening can be used to strengthen materials. This is the case with the majority of aluminum alloys used commercially today. Conversely, if the coarsening process proceeds too long the material can weaken. This occurs in jet turbine blades and is one of the reasons why turbine blades must be replaced after a certain number of hours of service. Thus developing accurate models of the coarsening process is central to creating a wide range of new materials encompassing those used in automobiles to those used in space applications.

docs.title: Aerosol Sampling Experiment
passages: Research area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter

Aerosols are small particles suspended in the air, and in Earth’s atmosphere, aerosols include soot, dust, pollen and a wide range of other natural and human-made materials. Smoke does not rise and dust does not settle in microgravity the way they do on Earth, causing aerosols to behave differently and pose hazards for crew members breathing the air. The Aerosol Sampling Experiment (ASE) collects airborne particles in the International Space Station’s (ISS) cabin air, and returns them to Earth for scientists to study.

The objectives of ASE were: 1- Characterize airborne particulate matter aboard the ISS to assess air quality for crew health and hardware longevity. 2- Identify particle sources (e.g., human skin, equipment wear, biological contaminants) in the spacecraft environment. 3- Improve understanding of particle transport and accumulation in microgravity conditions. 4- Support design of future spacecraft air filtration systems, ensuring they are appropriately targeted for actual airborne particle profiles.

Airborne particulate matter aboard the ISS exhibits a different size distribution, composition, and transport behavior in microgravity compared to Earth-based environments, and that particles from crew activity and hardware wear contribute significantly to the aerosol burden as well as the assumption that microgravity reduces sedimentation, allowing finer particles to stay suspended longer and accumulate in regions not typically affected by gravity-based settling on Earth.

The ASE approach involved passive aerosol sampling in multiple ISS modules using filters placed in air ducts and cabin areas (especially near high-traffic zones and vents) by deploying commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) samplers for long-duration exposure (3 months–1 year). The sampled filters were returned to Earth for ground-based analysis using: 1- Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), 2- Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) and 3- Gravimetric analysis. The ISS samples were compared to terrestrial cleanroom and indoor environments to assess relative cleanliness and particle source uniqueness. Data collected was cross-referenced with previous ISS air monitoring efforts (e.g., TOCA, CCAA) to inform models of contaminant accumulation and mitigation.

Crew members on the ISS are breathing more or less the same fixed volume of air that has been on the ISS for years. There is no chance to get ‘fresh air’ as we do on Earth, but an advanced air revitalization system processes and cleans the air continuously. Crew members in space have complained of allergies and nose and eye irritation, which suggests the ISS cabin air has a high concentration of tiny particles that can be inhaled. The ISS filtration system is designed to remove these particles, but researchers have no way to verify the efficiency or cleanliness of the air. This investigation generates new data to characterize the quality of the air on the ISS, in terms of particles. Future space travelers may benefit from this data, as they can be used in the design and selection of particle detectors appropriate for low gravity. Long-term manned space missions need aerosol measurement capability to ensure crew health and comfort

The primary objectives of the PCS investigation were to successfully grow binary colloidal crystal alloy structures to monitor their nucleation and growth kinetics with static and dynamic light scattering, determine their structures using laser light crystallography and the properties of the superlattices using dynamic light scattering. In addition, the structure and dynamics of gel-like structures formed by colloid-polymer mixtures will be measured using static and dynamic light scattering and the ultimate equilibrium structures behavior of the mixture will be determined. Finally, large scale fractal colloid aggregates and gels will be grown to measure their mechanical properties using dynamic light scattering, and potentially the cell oscillation techniques.

The availability of microgravity will allow binary colloidal superlattices to be formed from different materials providing new insights into the nucleation and growth kinetics of binary colloidal crystal alloy and thereby establish the new field of “colloid engineering.” This work will unambiguously determine the equilibrium phase diagram for attractive colloidal particles where the attraction is induced by depletion effects through the addition of polymer. It will also provide important new insight into the transition between equilibrium and kinetically limited behavior, in the absence of sedimentation. Further, this investigation will also lead to the fabrication of fractal colloidal structures that extend over the largest range of length scales ever produced, providing a critical test of our understanding of the formation of these structures. With such extended structures, it will be possible to study their physical properties and determine the consequences of the scale invariance on the properties. It will determine the fundamental limits of the range over which fractal structures can exist.

For binary colloidal crystal alloy the samples will consist of polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) particles, stabilized by a thin coating of poly-12-hydroxystearic acid, and suspended in a mixture of decalin and tetralin adjusted to exactly match the index of refraction of the PMMA. Once in orbit, the samples will be homogenized by rapidly spinning each sample cell and suddenly stopping it. Subsequent to homogenization, the nucleation and growth of the binary colloidal alloy crystallites will be monitored by static light scatter in the forward direction. The small angle light scattering will be complemented by larger angle scattering examining the Bragg reflections of the crystals. For the colloidal-polymer mixture part of the investigation the colloidal particles will again be PMMA spheres suspended in an index matched fluid. The volume fractions of these samples will range from about 1% to 30%. The polymer will be polystyrene, with a molecular weight ranging from about 100,000 to 1,000,000. The colloid-polymer mixtures will be homogenized using the same procedure used for the binary colloid mixtures. Immediately after they are homogenized, the small angle scattering will be monitored

The long term goal of this research is to establish a new method of fabricating materials, “Colloid Engineering,” where novel materials are fabricated using colloidal particles as precursors. With appropriate choices of the sizes of the particles, it should be possible to form colloidal alloy crystals of higher volume fraction than can be made with monodisperse particles. These colloidal alloys may form the precursors for very high quality ceramics. Alternatively, the particles could be made from different materials, forming colloidal superlattices with novel properties. Then, for example, one set of particles could be plastic and the other set of particles could be a metal or a semiconductor. Alternatively, these structures may be useful in forming materials with reduced phase space available for radiation, allowing a much simpler way of fabricating structures which possess photonic band gaps. Colloid engineering may offer a simple method for making these materials that completely bypasses the difficulties faced by traditional lithography techniques. The superlattices could also be used as novel optical switches or displays.

The primary objectives are: 1. Investigations of nucleation of crystal phases from supercooled (metastable) liquids as a function of stirring (fluid-flow) conditions. Systematic studies of this under terrestrial conditions are not possible due to the presence of convective flow in the liquid. 2. Measurements of thermophysical properties of metallic liquids under microgravity conditions, including the specific heat, viscosity, surface tension. These are then compared with measurements made under terrestrial conditions, when possible. These data are important for the analysis of the nucleation data, fluid flow calculations; additionally they are important for understanding fundamental connections between liquid dynamics and structure.

When the composition of the nucleating crystal phase is different from that of the liquid, long range diffusion can become important for the nucleation process. The potential impact on the nucleation rate depends on the ratio of the attachment rates to the nucleating cluster and the time required for long-range diffusion. This can be investigated by nucleation measurements made as a function of stirring, since fluid-flow can decrease the impact of long-range diffusion.

Measurements of the supercooling are made under controlled stirring conditions. The nucleation rates are derived from the distribution of maximum supercooling following the approach developed by Skripov. By systematically changing the fluid-flow rates by applying controlled voltages to the heater/positioner coils in the ESA electromagnetic levitation facility on the ISS (ISS-EML), the nucleation rates can be studied as function of stirring, allowing the hypothesis to be examined.

Realistic modeling approaches have the potential to greatly improve the efficiency of materials development. However, progress is frequently hampered by the lack of relevant thermophysical property data needed for the modeling. Further, key processes such as crystal nucleation from the liquid or other phase transitions within the liquid, are often poorly understood, making it difficult to realistically model them. In many cases, the experimental data and a deeper understanding of some processes cannot be obtained from terrestrial experiments due to interactions with sample containers at the temperatures of interest. The combination of the containerless based terrestrial methods and the ISS-EML enables these measurements. In addition to their relevance for processes such as additive manufacturing on earth, where nucleation in highly stirred conditions is important, measurements in two different gravitational fields will be important for designing additive manufacturing in space and on the Moon.

The primary objective of the Strata-1 investigation was to study the mixing and segregation dynamics of regolith on small bodies by exposing a suite of regolith simulants to the microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) for a period of one year. In response to variable gravity levels and ambient vibrational environment the Strata-1 experiment aimed to investigate the behavior of regolith simulants specifically chosen to represent models of regolith covering a range of complexity and tailored to inform and improve computational studies.

By utilizing the prolonged microgravity and vibrational conditions of ISS as analogues to those on small Solar System bodies, the Strata-1 investigation aims to answer fundamental questions about how regolith evolves on planetary bodies and what roles particle density, shape, and composition play in the evolution of regolith dynamics.

The Strata-1 experiment consisted of four evacuated tubes partially filled with regolith simulants.The simulants, namely, glass beads, glass shards, meteorite, and carbonaceous chondrite, were chosen to represent models of regolith covering a range of complexity and tailored to inform and improve computational studies. The four tubes are regularly imaged while moving in response to the ambient vibrational environment using dedicated cameras. The imagery is then downlinked to the Strata-1 science team about every two months. Analyses performed on the imagery includes evaluating the extent of the segregation of Strata-1 samples and comparing the observations to computational models. After Strata-1's return to Earth, x-ray tomography and optical microscopy will be used to study the post-flight simulant distribution. There two simulation methods that have been proposed for this research are the Soft-sphere Discrete Element Method (SSDEM) and the Contact Dynamics Method (CD).

Strata-1 supports the space exploration program by enabling new interpretation of a wide range of NASA missions including but not limited to Stardust, Deep Impact; EPOXI, Near Earth Asteroid Rendezvous (NEAR), OSIRISREx and Hayabusa-1 and -2. The new Strata information on regolith behavior and mechanics directly assists planning for the Asteroid Redirect Mission ARM), the OSIRIS-REx mission, In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) efforts on small bodies, and upcoming NASA missions to comets and asteroids. The Strata-1 study advances our fundamental understanding of the mechanical behavior of loose material. Results may find utility in any application that involves the mixing of dry materials, such as pharmaceutical tablet manufacture, the study of dune migration and dynamics, and similar fields.

The Ring-Sheared Drop (RSD) is a Microgravity Science Glovebox experiment that launched in July 2019 to the ISS to study shearing flow in the absence of solid walls. The major goals of this project were to adapt and use the RSD module to develop and test predictive models of non-Newtonian flow of high-concentration proteins at the interface. Incorporating non-Newtonian constitutive equations for both interfacial and bulk flows and coupling the interfacial and bulk stresses is essential for mechanistic models that would be capable of predicting behavior under flow conditions of practical interest. The coupled problem is intrinsically nonlinear and there is a need to develop robust and accurate numerical techniques to interrogate flow dynamics and experimentally validate and verify results. The ring-sheared drop interfacial bioprocessing of pharmaceuticals-I (RSD-IBP-I) campaign aimed to study non-Newtonian interfacial hydrodynamics of the blood transport proteins bovine serum albumin (BSA) and human serum albumin (HSA) in microgravity. Specifically, scientific aims focus on the effects of protein primary structure (BSA or HSA), protein concentration (4, 40, or 400 mg/mL), and interf

The study of fluid interfaces coupled to bulk flows, including non-Newtonian response of either the interfacial or the bulk fluid can be uniquely advanced through experimentation in microgravity, where surface tension containment can be achieved at relatively large length scales. If the hydrodynamics of concentrated protein solutions are precisely measured, then sufficiently descriptive viscosity constitutive relations can be selected or developed from fundamental physics to describe fluid behavior.

Preflight preparation included refurbishment of all test cells including modification of test cells S/N 101-106 to include the flight tested (both parabolic and ISS with the assistance of NASA MSFC) integrated deployment tube and upper ring design by TBE, refurbishment of all test cells used in the previous RSD-BPS campaign by TBE, preparation of protein samples and methodological ground controls.

Following sample installation, the RSD drop was deployed by extruding a drop from the deployment tube until pinning is achieved at the far ring. Shearing was then commenced by rotation of the far ring, measurements recorded for startup, steady, and stop flows each at 3, 10, and 30 rpm. Each 1.5 min. image sequence was then compressed to a portable video file and downlinked to the ground computer at RPI. ISS flight campaigns occurred Summer 2022 and Spring 2023, achieving 92% of proposed science objectives with 121.5/132 sample videos successfully collected, meeting the criteria for complete success. Additionally, 27 videos of interfacial aging and 24 micrographs of extra data were collected. The RSD hardware concluded the campaign in a nominal configuration with good health and status after four years in space aboard the ISS.

Postflight: Test cells were returned June 30th 2023 on SpX-28 to TBE. Test cells appear to be in nominal pre-refurbishment configuration. RSD hardware remains in nominal configuration and good health.

Coupled bulk and interfacial flow in the RSD, developed under this grant is currently being analyzed to aid in formulating a model of non-Newtonian interfacial hydrodynamics coupled to a Newtonian bulk flow. These results were recently submitted for publication in a special issue of the journal Fluids, entitled ''Non-Newtonian Flow: Interfacial and Bulk Phenomena.'' While all cases examined remain at least weakly coupled to the bulk flow, this investigation established the effective ranges of model parameters. Bulk flow profiles demonstrate moderate sensitivity of the bulk flow to the behavior of the air-liquid interface, in general increasing with higher Boussinesq number Bq (non-dimensionalized surface viscosity) while maintaining interface to bulk flow coupling.
