The objectives are to quantify phase separation efficiency in wedge channels as a function of flow parameters, bubble characteristics, and channel geometry; determine the influence of bubble size and injection frequency on separation efficiency; and optimize wedge geometry for passive phase separation.

The hypothesis underlying CCF-PS EU2 is that specific wedge and gapped-wedge channel designs can passively separate liquid and gas phases due to the complex interplay of capillary and inertial forces. Furthermore, it is hypothesized that by carefully adjusting flow conditions, such as flow rate and channel length as well as bubble properties, such as bubble size and frequency, it is possible to identify geometries and regimes suitable for gas-liquid separation, which can be used for spacecraft tank design and liquid supply.

Building upon the CF-CV EU2 approach, the phase separation investigation utilizes a controlled bubble injection system to introduce bubbles of varying sizes and frequencies upstream of the wedge channel. The microgravity environment of the ISS ensures capillary-dominated flow conditions. Systematic variation of bubble injection parameters (size, frequency, location), flow rate, and channel geometry (wedge angle, length) enables comprehensive mapping of phase separation efficiency. High-speed imaging (HSHRC) coupled with wider-view video (MSGC) allows for detailed observation and quantification of bubble migration and coalescence. Image analysis techniques are employed to track bubble trajectories, quantify bubble size distributions before and after the wedge channel, and determine the overall degree of gas-liquid separation. This quantitative data is then correlated with the varied parameters to assess the effectiveness of the wedge geometry for passive phase separation and to optimize design parameters for enhanced performance.

Current spacecraft fuel tanks rely on an additional reservoir to prevent gases from entering the engines during firing. Capillary systems larger than a few millimeters in length are impossible to study on the ground, but the weightlessness on the International Space Station makes research on a variety of capillary channel sizes possible. The results are useful for the design and testing of liquid management systems in current use and for future missions. Rocket fuel tank designs and construction models from space research help to advance new technology and manufacturing capabilities on Earth.

docs.title: Plant Water Management
passages: Keywords: Root aeration · plant growth · Capillary-driven irrigation · Gas-liquid separation · Passive irrigation systems · Hydroponics · Life-support systems · Controlled-environment agriculture
The primary objectives of the Plant Water Management (PWM) experiments were to:

a) Experimentally characterize and validate the use of passive capillary and geometric control for plant watering in microgravity. The research quantified the stability limits of capillary-driven flow under varying conditions, evaluated aeration and bubble management performance within root-zone analogs, and assessed start-up, shutdown, and drainage behaviors of the fluidic system on orbit and also correlated observed flow regimes and saturation levels with computational capillary flow models to improve predictive design tools for reduced-gravity systems. b) Advance the PWM technology toward higher Technology Readiness Levels (TRL), demonstrating reliable, scalable configurations for integration into future space-based plant growth habitats. The resulting data and models informed the design of next-generation, low-mass, low-power life-support and food-production systems for long-duration missions on the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

This research was based on the hypothesis that, in microgravity where gravity-driven fluid behavior is absent, capillary forces, surface tension, and geometric design could provide reliable water and nutrient delivery to plant root zones. Passive physical mechanisms replaced gravity in distributing and reclaiming fluids within the growth systems. Surface-wetting characteristics and channel geometry were designed to maintain root-zone hydration, facilitate aeration, and manage liquid–gas separation without pumps or active components. These mechanisms sustained water availability and oxygen exchange, preventing oversaturation or desiccation. The approach demonstrated that passive capillary systems could support consistent, low-maintenance plant watering and aeration in reduced-gravity environments.

PWM employed passive capillary-based fluidic systems to deliver water and nutrients to plant root zones under microgravity aboard the ISS. Growth modules were designed with controlled channel geometries and surface-wetting properties to direct liquid flow, manage gas-liquid separation, and maintain root-zone aeration. Both hydroponic and soil-based configurations were tested to evaluate performance across different growth media. Measurements included monitoring liquid distribution, root-zone moisture levels, aeration efficiency, and bubble formation, alongside comparing observations to predictive capillary flow models. By systematically varying system geometry, wetting conditions, and operational parameters, the experiments defined design guidelines for robust, low-maintenance plant growth systems for space and analogous terrestrial applications.

Demonstrating passive fluid management in plant growth systems is enabling reliable water and nutrient delivery in microgravity, supporting long-duration space missions. Advancing capillary-based irrigation is reducing system mass, complexity, and power requirements. In relation to agriculture on Earth, results from this research are improving precision irrigation, conserving water, and enhancing root-zone aeration in hydroponic and soil systems. Generating validated models of capillary-driven flow is guiding efficient, resilient plant growth technologies. Supporting scalable, low-maintenance systems is fostering innovations in both space life-support and sustainable food production on Earth.

Keywords: USML-1 · STDCE-1 · thermocapillary flow · buoyancy · Columbia · Surface Tension · Constant Flux · Marangoni Number

The main objectives of STDCE-1 are to investigate: -The extent and nature of thermocapillary flows in transient periods as well as under steady conditions. -Temperature distributions along the free surface and in the bulk fluid. -The effect of the heating mode and the heating level on the flows. -The effect of the liquid free surface on the flows -The onset conditions and nature of oscillatory flows

The STDCE program employed a comprehensive and multifaceted approach to investigate the complexities of thermocapillary flow. This strategy encompassed a combination of theoretical analysis, numerical modeling, ground-based experiments, and ultimately, microgravity experiments aboard the Space Shuttle.

Theoretical Analysis Dimensionless Parameters: Researchers derived and identified the key dimensionless parameters governing thermocapillary flow, including the Marangoni number (Ma), Prandtl number (Pr), aspect ratio (Ar), and the novel surface deformation parameter (S). These parameters facilitated the understanding of the relative importance of different forces and physical mechanisms at play and provided a framework for data analysis and comparison.

Scaling Laws: By analyzing the governing equations and boundary conditions, scientists established scaling laws that characterized the behavior of key flow features, such as boundary layer thicknesses and velocity scales. This theoretical groundwork offered valuable insights into the expected flow characteristics under different conditions.

Numerical Modeling Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD): Sophisticated CFD models were developed to simulate thermocapillary flow behavior under various conditions. These models accounted for factors such as heat transfer, fluid properties, surface tension effects, and free surface deformation. The numerical simulations provided detailed predictions of flow patterns, velocity distributions, and temperature profiles, serving as a basis for comparison with experimental data and for exploring a wider range of parameters than feasible experimentally.

Ground-Based Experiments Reduced-Gravity Simulations: Researchers conducted experiments in drop towers and other reduced-gravity facilities to observe thermocapillary flows under conditions with minimized buoyancy effects. These experiments served as a stepping stone towards the microgravity experiments and provided preliminary data for model validation and refinement.

Test Fluid and Hardware Development: Extensive ground-based testing was undertaken to optimize the experimental setup, including the selection of the test fluid (silicone oil), the design of the test cell, and the development of flow visualization and temperature measurement techniques.

Microgravity Experiments Space Shuttle Missions: The culmination of the research effort involved conducting the STDCE experiments aboard the Space Shuttle, taking advantage of the extended microgravity environment to study thermocapillary flows over a broader range of parameters and conditions than possible on Earth. This included meticulous execution of the test matrix, encompassing various heating modes, power levels, and free surface shapes, while collecting detailed flow visualization and temperature data.

Data Analysis and Model Validation Comparison of Results: The experimental data from both ground-based and microgravity experiments were rigorously analyzed and compared with the predictions from numerical models. This iterative process allowed for the assessment of model accuracy, the identification of areas for improvement, and ultimately, a deeper understanding of the fundamental physics driving thermocapillary flow.

While the STDCE program was primarily driven by the need to understand and predict thermocapillary flow behavior in microgravity environments, its findings and technological advancements have yielded valuable insights and applications for Earth-based processes as well.

Enhanced Understanding of Thermocapillary Flows Fundamental Physics: STDCE significantly advanced the understanding of the fundamental physics governing thermocapillary flows, including the interplay between surface tension gradients, heat transfer, and fluid motion. This knowledge provides a solid foundation for tackling complex fluid flow problems in various terrestrial applications.

Numerical Model Refinement: The experimental data from STDCE served as a critical benchmark for validating and refining numerical models used to predict thermocapillary flow behavior. These improved models now offer more accurate and reliable predictions for a wider range of applications, both in space and on Earth.

Technological Advancements Non-Intrusive Measurement Techniques: The development and refinement of non-intrusive measurement techniques, such as infrared imaging and particle image velocimetry, for the STDCE have expanded the toolkit for studying fluid flows in various settings. These techniques are now widely employed in research and industrial applications on Earth, including the study of combustion processes, crystal growth, and microfluidics.

Flow Visualization and Analysis: The advanced flow visualization and analysis methods developed for STDCE have facilitated the study of complex flow patterns and structures in various terrestrial applications. These tools enable researchers and engineers to gain deeper insights into flow dynamics and optimize processes for improved efficiency and performance.

Earth-Based Applications Materials Processing: The insights gained from STDCE have direct relevance to materials processing techniques on Earth, particularly those involving free surfaces and high-temperature gradients, such as welding, crystal growth, and the fabrication of thin films and coatings. Understanding and controlling thermocapillary flows in these processes can lead to improved product quality and reduced defect formation.

Microfluidics: The knowledge gained from STDCE is applicable to the burgeoning field of microfluidics, where surface tension forces play a dominant role in manipulating and controlling fluids at the microscale. This has implications for the development of microfluidic devices for applications such as drug delivery, medical diagnostics, and chemical analysis.

Overall, the STDCE program, while initially motivated by the challenges of microgravity research, has generated valuable knowledge and technological advancements with far-reaching implications for various Earth-based applications. The enhanced understanding of thermocapillary flow and the development of advanced measurement and analysis techniques have contributed to the advancement of materials processing, microfluidics, and numerous other fields, demonstrating the profound impact of fundamental scientific research on both space exploration and terrestrial technology.

This project investigated the high-temperature thermophysical properties of molten metal oxides, with a particular focus on molten titanates. These property measurements were used to establish correlations with atomic structure and glass formation.

The research exploits the unique capabilities in microgravity to measure the thermophysical properties – density, thermal expansion coefficient, viscosity and surface tension – over a wide temperature range. Samples, including glasses, were recovered after melt processing in microgravity for ground-based analysis and comparison with materials made on Earth. The work underpins development of a materials property-structure data set that can help in development of new materials and in meeting requirements of material utilization, processing in space, and exploration.

Glasses are inherently non-equilibrium materials. Their structure and properties depend directly on the processing route used to form them. Because gravity affects fluid convection, glass formation and resulting structure may differ between different gravity conditions. We hypothesize that the superior control of fluid and thermal transport possible in microgravity will enable improved glass forming ability via melt quenching in containerless conditions, particularly for highly fragile liquid oxides. We hypothesize that the differences in thermal history - between microgravity and Earth-based processing - will manifest as differences in structure and thermodynamic properties.

Density, thermal expansion, viscosity, and surface tension of molten oxides were measured using the Electrostatic Levitation Furnace (ELF) onboard the ISS. Measurements included silhouette imaging and drop oscillation over a wide range of temperatures, including deep supercooling.

Recovered samples included glasses and polycrystalline materials, which were characterized post-flight using a combination of X-ray scattering, neutron scattering, X-ray tomography, Raman spectroscopy, calorimetry, and electron microscopy. Space-made glasses were compared with terrestrial analogues to investigate how changes in fluid transport may influence structure and properties.

This project advances the understanding of oxide melt properties, atomic structure, and glass formation. This builds a foundation for the development of new functional glasses and related technologies, with applications on Earth and in space for exploration and utilization of local resources.

The project was successful on several fronts: 1. Microgravity experiments enabled melting, drop imaging, drop oscillation and measurements of properties of approximately 30 samples. 2. First experiments in ELF that used melt processing to make and recover glass in space. 3. First publications that compare the structure of glasses made in microgravity vs. terrestrially. 4. First demonstration of laser action in a titanate-network glass and of a glass made by containerless processing. 5. Results were analyzed in collaboration with a variety of researchers leading to 12 peer-reviewed publications and more than 20 presentations. 6. Two patents are pending based on results of the work. These have a high impact on glass materials processing in space and development of new glass products both on-Earth and in reduced gravity. 7. The project met all of the stated goals: perform basic research in microgravity, develop applied knowledge to make new materials, build collaborations to advance the field, and establish the basis for new glass materials products made in reduced gravity. 8. Keywords: Perfect Crystals · lymphoma · Crystallography · Radiation · MnSOD · Cancer · Protein Crystals

The Perfect Crystals investigation uses microgravity environment on the International Space Station to grow crystals of human manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD). This sheds light on how the antioxidant protein helps protect the human body from oxidizing radiation and oxides created as a byproduct of metabolism. For best results, the analysis technique requires large crystals with minimal imperfections, which are more easily produced in the microgravity environment of the space station.

In 2001, the Borgstahl laboratory successfully grew large crystals of SOD using microgravity conditions on the International Space Station (ISS). Using existing crystallization hardware that uses the Granada Crystallization Boxes (GCB) for capillary counter diffusion protocols will be used to achieve microgravity crystallization results for SOD. The principal outcome will be to identify the role of hydrogen atoms in enzymatic activity, discern superoxide from peroxide, and water from hydroxide ion by their protonation state and decipher a structure-based mechanism for human MnSOD more precisely than from previous X-ray crystallographic models determined from Earth-grown crystals.

The Growth of Large, Perfect Protein Crystals for Neutron Crystallography investigation grows perfect, large-volume crystal suitable for neutron macromolecular crystallography of large unit cell protein crystals in microgravity. The protein of study in this investigation is human manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD or SOD2), which has an enzymatic mechanism that relies on a proton shuttling pattern that has yet to be fully elucidated. Neutron macromolecular crystallography allows for visualization of protons that cannot be achieved by XRay Diffraction or Cryo-EM, but requires large-volume crystals minimal imperfection for best results. Gravity has been implicated as a cause of defects in crystals grown on Earth. The marriage of the liquid-liquid capillary diffusion crystal growth technique to the microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) allows for the growth of multiple greater than 1 mm3 crystals with very few defects. Please refer to AccessingPerfectCrystalData.pdf under the Science Documents section.

Manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) is implicated in a number of human diseases, including non-Hodgkins lymphoma, lung cancer and colorectal cancer. Understanding how it works is an important step toward developing better prevention and treatment methods for such diseases. In space application, MnSOD could help researchers protect astronauts on future long-term missions. Astronauts receive significantly more exposure to oxidizing radiation than people on Earth, and on long journeys such as to Mars may receive dangerous doses that create Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS). These can damage DNA and other biomolecules, causing diseases such as cancer. The manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) enzyme converts ROS into molecular oxygen and hydrogen peroxide, which other enzymes can then break down. Studies on MnSOD can help researchers can develop artificial techniques to reduce ROS and help protect astronauts on future long-term missions.

The overarching goal of the project was to gain a better fundamental understanding of the relationship between bijel morphology, rheology, mechanical stability, and processability through combined ground-based and microgravity experiments and theoretical calculations.

This investigation hypothesizes that interparticle interactions have a profound impact on the rheology of bijel particulate suspensions and attempts to answer the fundamental scientific question as to how the various forces at the colloidal scale are affected by Marangoni convection in microgravity. The nature of interparticle interactions and its impact on rheology has profound implications for the processability of bijels and the ability to transform them into functional materials.

Mixtures of propylene glycol/nitroethane (PG/NE) at their critical composition were prepared. Partially hydrophobic silica particles were suspended in the PG/NE mixture and the suspensions were filled in different cuvettes. On orbit, these cuvettes were heated to 25C, mixed in-situ, and then quenched from 25C to 0C. Following the quench, an imaging protocol was used to collect a stack of 100 images in the Z direction at a spacing of 5 mm.

The ability to design and fabricate the unique 3-dimensional bijel structures opens a wide spectrum of new structures for applications that can benefit from synthesis of hierarchically porous monoliths and composites with a spinodal-like microstructure in which every constituent phase is naturally continuous throughout the entire sample volume. This type of tailored porous microstructures can improve the physical properties and performance of materials used in a number of space and terrestrial applications. Space exploration applications include improved energy storage batteries and fuel cells, and catalytic microreactors for lower mass and volume designs in spacecraft life support and ISRU systems. The primary objective of this investigation was to understand the effect of microgravity processing on composition and microstructure evolution in metallic glass forming alloys or bulk metallic glass (BMG). Specific questions to be answered were:

(a) How does processing in microgravity change the composition of the matrix of the glass-forming alloys compared to processing in gravity? (b) How does the volume fraction of the W spheres affect the composition and properties of the matrix? (c) How does the composition and viscosity of the glass-forming alloy affect the diffusion of W in microgravity? (d) How do the different diameter of W spheres affect the diffusion of W into the matrix? (e) Does the dissolved W provide a mechanism to improve the wear resistance and toughness of the matrix by providing reinforcement for brittle phases?

The hypothesis for the experiment is that microgravity promotes composite formation by stabilizing the interface between the W nano-particle nuclei and the bulk liquid. In contrast, on Earth, the heavy W particles would fall out of the system as they form. Therefore, the composition of the solid formed on Earth will differ from that formed in microgravity.

On Earth, the samples should solidify in a manner consistent with the Scheil solidification approximation meaning: (a) liquid diffusion is instant over experimental timescales (b) solid-state diffusion does not occur (solid falls out of the system as it forms) (c) the solid composition profile will follow the solidus as the system cools, until all the liquid is consumed.

In contrast, in microgravity, the solid/liquid interface lifetime is much longer, so there is more opportunity for solid back-diffusion. For this case, the composition profile will approach (but not reach) that of the equilibrium solidification case. After processing in both gravity and microgravity, experimental compositional data at the matrix-sphere interface will be obtained. It is expected that composites formed on Earth will solidify consistent with Scheil solidification and composites formed in microgravity will deviate from Scheil, approaching equilibrium solidification.

The objective of the flight experiment is to process 12 samples of two glass-forming alloys (Vitreloy 106 and Zr48Cu47.5Al4Co0.5) in microgravity with three different volume fractions of W spheres (5%, 15% and 30%) with two different diameters of W spheres (25-36 μm diameter and 140-150 μm diameter). The cast composite samples were 15 mm in diameter and 12 mm long cylinders. The W particles were distributed as homogeneously as possible without sedimentation. On orbit, the samples were loaded into the Low Gradient Furnace (LGF) on the Materials Science Research Rack. They were held for 120 minutes at 1,200 °C (1,473 K) in microgravity with the intent to dissolve the W particles into the matrix and to create a fine distribution of W dendrites homogenously distributed throughout. The samples were then cooled back to room temperature slowly, solidifying the morphology and composition. The Vitreloy 106 samples were compared with Zr48Cu47.5Al4Co0.5 in terms of composition of the matrix, morphology of the W dendrites, and mechanical properties, with comparisons drawn between samples produced on-orbit and on the ground to distinguish the effects of microgravity.

The development of innovative new materials is a fundamental part of future terrestrial and space technologies. These materials have a tremendous benefit towards improving life on Earth, from improving the accessibility and cost of solar power, to making cars safer and stronger, to reducing the mass of aircraft, for example. Innovative technologies typically require new materials tailored for those applications. This drives materials development.

There are both technology demonstration objectives and scientific objectives. The technology demonstration objectives are to test the performance of an automatically moving baffle in microgravity and to determine the behavior and possible advantages of liquid encapsulation in microgravity conditions.The science objectives are to visualize the melt/encapsulant behavior in microgravity and to grow doped InSb without dewetting. The key goal of SUBSA was to clarify the origin of the melt convection in space and to reduce the magnitude to the point that it does not interfere with the transport phenomena.

A baffle placed inside a melt reduces the effective size of the melt and leads to a decrease in the amount of convection. The combined effect of microgravity (reduction of gravitational acceleration by a factor of 10^6 ) and a small zone melt (reduction of the size and temperature differential by a factor of 10^3 ) will generate the effective conditions of “nano-gravity” (the Rayleigh number will be reduced by a factor of 10^9 ).

In the space environment, accelerations produce circular motions that affect the solidification of crystal growth/semiconductor materials flight experiments, resulting in a material that is less useful.The objectives of SUBSA are:Test the performance of an automatically moving baffle (used to minimize melt motion).Visualization of the melting process to identify what causes the melt motion.Production of several crystals with reproducible properties.To determine the behavior and possible advantages of liquid encapsulation in microgravity conditions.

The SUBSA furnace, with its capability to control and visualize melting and solidification of semiconductor crystals has increased our understanding of semiconductor crystal growth phenomena. The transparent furnace coupled with the video downlink and real-time commanding capability provided a powerful tool for scientists to watch the motion of the crystal-melt interface as semiconductor crystals were formed. The design of the SUBSA ampoule which includes a baffle and a system that prevents de-wetting resulted in crystals whose properties have not been disrupted by micro-accelerations at the Station, making it possible for future researchers to produce the high-quality semiconductor crystals that are in demand on Earth.

docs.title: Capillary Flow Experiment
passages: Keywords: Capillary Flow Experiment (CFE) · Capillary forces · CFE

1. The primary objective of the CL unit experiments is to identify the extent the role of the boundary condition at the contact line plays in the natural dynamic response of a large capillary interface to a variety of disturbances. 2. The primary objective of the ICF units is to experimentally determine secondary imbibition rates in complex containers due to spontaneous large length scale capillary flows along interior corners in weakly 3-dimensional containers. Secondary objectives of the experiments are to quantify such flows in closed loop cycles, and to identify the passive phase separation characteristics of certain capillary driven multiphase-flows (e.g. bubbly flow) along interior corners. 3. The primary objective of the VG units is to determine equilibrium interface configurations and critical wetting conditions for interfaces between interior corners separated by a gap. A secondary objective is to validate numerical predictions of the large length scale discontinuous or nearly discontinuous wetting phenomena.

The CFE investigations operate under the hypothesis that capillary phenomena in microgravity, specifically contact line dynamics, interior corner flows, and vane-gap wetting, deviate significantly from idealized theoretical predictions based on simplified geometries and boundary conditions. This deviation is anticipated to manifest as measurable differences in dynamic interface response (frequency and damping) for varying contact line conditions, geometry-dependent secondary imbibition rates in complex containers, and distinct critical wetting conditions in vane-wall gaps influenced by gap size and wettability. The CFE experiments are designed to quantify these deviations, providing empirical data to refine existing theoretical models and enhance the predictive capabilities for low-gravity fluid management systems.

Without gravity, it is more difficult to control the flow of fluids and this is a challenge for designing spacecraft systems such as liquid propellants/cryogens, thermal control systems, wastewater management and recycling.Capillary forces (the interaction of liquid with solid that can draw a fluid up a narrow tube) continue to act in the absence of gravity and can be exploited to control fluid orientation so that fluid systems on spacecraft perform predictably.CFE uses the low-gravity environment provided by the International Space Station to understand the special dynamics of capillary flow and will aid in the design of fluid transport systems on future spacecraft.

The knowledge gained from this payload has the potential to be instrumental in the design of future fluid systems for spacecraft-impacting fluid bearing containers such as propellant and cryogenic fluids tanks, thermal control system coolant reservoirs, water storage and management systems, liquid state low-gravity materials processing equipment, and biofluids handling instruments for inflight human health systems. By performing this experiment, researchers will gain information that will lead to improvements in system reliability with reductions in system mass and complexity. These applications of CFE are in direct support of NASA's mission to develop safe, reliable, and affordable spacecraft to pursue the greater exploration of our solar system and universe. The results of the flight experiments are also expected to provide insights into terrestrial interfacial phenomena and may lead to models predicting fluid flows in porous media (i.e. ground water transport), complex capillary structures (i.e. high performance wicks for heat pipes employed in electronics cooling), and Lab-On-Chip technologies (i.e., microscale biofluids processing).

The main goal of this experiment is to demonstrate in a space environment, a prototype system that produces USP grade SWI, and mixes the SWI with sterile USP sodium chloride to produce a homogeneous Normal Saline IV fluid. The experiment shall also demonstrate at least one bubble removal apparatus, as this is a critical step to prevent delivering harmful gas emboli to patients when the deployed system is used. The system will utilize a single flow rate, determined by the maximum volume/hour required for a worst-case-scenario medical event.

It is hypothesized that a prototype system, utilizing deionization, magnetic stirring, and bubble separation techniques, can effectively produce USP-compliant normal saline solution from readily available spacecraft potable water sources in a microgravity environment.

The IVGEN investigation employs a comprehensive and well-structured approach to demonstrate and validate the feasibility of producing IV fluids in space. The approach encompasses a combination of on-orbit experimentation, ground-based testing, and meticulous data analysis, as summarized below:

On-Orbit Experimentation: The core of the investigation involves a flight experiment onboard the International Space Station (ISS), utilizing a prototype IV fluid generation system. This experiment simulates the conditions and constraints of a space mission, allowing for direct testing of the system's performance in a microgravity environment.

Ground-Based Testing: Prior to the flight experiment, a rigorous ground-based test program is conducted to: -Concept Verification: Validate the design and performance of key system components, such as the bubble separators and mixers, in both normal and reduced gravity environments. -Input Water Analysis: Characterize the quality of potential water sources, including ISS potable water and various CEV water sources, to ensure the system's compatibility and effectiveness. -Temperature Effects: Assess the impact of varying temperatures on the system's performance, particularly on the DI cartridge and the conductivity sensors.

Data Acquisition and Analysis: During the on-orbit experiment, a comprehensive dataset is collected, including: -Environmental Data: Temperature, pressure, and acceleration measurements to understand the system's operating environment and potential impact on performance. -System Performance Data: Conductivity, flow rate, and image data to assess the purification, mixing, and bubble removal processes.
Post-Flight Sample Analysis: The two 1.5-liter bags of NS produced on orbit are returned to Earth for rigorous testing by a certified laboratory, ensuring the produced IV fluid meets USP standards.

Data Interpretation and Scaling: The collected data is meticulously analyzed to: -Validate System Performance: Confirm the successful production of USP-compliant NS solution in microgravity. -Identify Challenges and Limitations: Assess potential issues and areas for improvement based on observed system behavior. -Enable System Scaling: Utilize the data to inform the design and development of a larger, operational system capable of meeting the needs of future exploration missions.

Due to mass and volume limitations, space vehicles cannot carry sufficient IV fluid for medical contingencies. A filtering and mixing system that can make IV fluid in situ would provide the treatment capability without the mass and volume constraints. IVGEN was designed and will be tested to meet that need. IVGEN technology could be used on Earth to generate IV fluid in Third World countries where medical resources are limited.

In ACE-T9, the imaging capability, folding dynamics, and assembly behavior of linear colloidal chains, colloidal dimers, and lock-and-key particles were studied by the combination of a proper design of particle architecture and tunable colloidal interactions (e.g., double layer repulsion and hydrophobic attraction). In the case of colloidal chains, for example, the single chain dynamics should sensitively depend on the chain flexibility and monomer-solvent interactions. Under the microgravity environment, we hoped to observe qualitative three-dimensional, real-time dynamics of single colloidal chains (using pre-confocal - bright field and fluorescent microscopy. We also aimed to observe three-dimensional structures assembled from colloidal dimers and lock-and-key particles and to measure the binding equilibrium constants that are impossible to measure in earth experiments due to the effect of sedimentation.

In the microgravity environment, we will study the folding dynamics of single colloidal chains where the chain architecture can be varied systematically, and the monomer-solvent interaction can be tuned by varying salt concentrations. Furthermore, by tuning the balance between electric double layer repulsion and hydrophobic attraction on both colloidal dimers and lock-and-key particles, we aim to study the assembly of those colloidal molecules into complex three-dimensional structures and measure the binding equilibrium constants. This set of experiments provide insight into the relation between particle shape, colloidal interaction and structure. With the wide variety of attributes that characterize anisotropic interactions, we will probe previously inaccessible regions of complex phase space. Our studies will move significantly beyond hard spheres and towards experimental models appropriate for studying fundamental questions associated with complex symmetries.

The imaging goal is to observe (1) real-time and three-dimensional particle centroid positions of colloidal chains over both short (30 minutes) and long period (one week); (2) assembled structures, crystallites, and resolve particle centroid positions for colloidal dimers and Janus spheres. For short-time imaging, the video should be taken with 5 fps over 30 minutes. For both cases, the x-y positions of particles should be determined with less than 5% error (with respect to particle diameter). The z-positions should be determined within 1 micron. For fluorescence imaging, lamp should be shuttered between image sets to prevent sample bleaching.

In-situ manipulation of anisotropic interactions and dynamic pathways, based on rational colloidal particle design and proper use of external fields, could lead to crystalline and a periodic structures beyond those seen in nature. Results from this study will lead to improved control of non-covalent assembly of molecules, efficient tailoring of lattice symmetries, and the scalable processing of nano-structured materials. The development of new colloidal molecules and their associated assembled structures have considerable technological impact as well. Such structures will generally lead to arrays with reduced symmetry and enhanced directionality. They can interact with a broad range of electromagnetic radiation in unique ways and can exhibit collective photonic, plasmonic, mechanical, electronic, or magnetic properties that are not manifested at the level of single particles. As a result, they have significant potential as next-generation functional materials.

Nanoparticle Haloing (NPH) is a colloidal stabilization technique that has been discovered relatively recently. In NPH, highly charged nanoparticles are used to stabilize much larger (by 2 orders of magnitude or more), non-charged particles. To accomplish this stabilization, the volume fraction of nanoparticles within the suspension need only be on the order of 1e-5 up to 1e-4 to stabilize at 1 to 2 vol% suspension of the larger particles.

The objective of this work is to gain fundamental insight into the physics of NPH with the aim of addressing the following unresolved questions: • How will NPH suspensions behave in thermal or electrical field gradients as they do under gravity? • How does the halo form or re-form if disturbed? • Can NPH (and manipulation thereof) be used to assemble and reconfigure colloidal crystals? • How does the nanoparticle charge impact halo formation?

When NPH suspensions were allowed to settle under gravity, those that were stabilized (while in suspension) formed highly ordered, 3-dimensional colloidal crystal structures. Current theory suggests that nanoparticles create a charge layer by forming a cage, or Halo, around the larger particles. Another hypothesis regarding the NPH stabilization mechanism focuses entirely on nanoparticle adsorption to the surface of the larger particle. Based on the measurement of the interaction forces between two larger colloidal surfaces in a nanoparticle suspension, it was found that the force curves obtained could be fitted using a model based on nanoparticle adsorption.
The ACE-T12 experiment utilizes the Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) and the Light Microscopy Module (LMM). The FIR is built to accommodate a wide range of experiments.

Accordingly, the ACE-T12 experiment included confocal microscopy, which used a 532-nm frequency-doubled Nd:YAG laser, a confocal scanner, and an 8- to 12-bit digital CCD camera on a Leica DM-RXA microscope. The scanner captured 30 frames per second of confocal images by the CCD camera.

ACE-T12 utilizes capillary cells. Three capillary cells with different concentrations of nanoparticles were provided in a sample module. Here is a brief high-level descriptive outline of the investigation on-orbit procedures that gives general experiment steps for each capillary. 1- Short mix of sample. 2- Ramp temperature to find critical temperature and reduce temperature and initiate a very long mix of sample. 3- Determine Region of Interest (ROI). 4- Ramp temperature continuously while imaging. 5- Mix sample followed by Single temperature step visits. 6- Mix sample followed by stepwise temperature ramp with image stacks.

Ultimately, the ability to design colloidal particles with a variety of well-controlled three-dimensional bonding symmetries opens a wide spectrum of new structures for colloidal self-assembly, beyond particle assemblies whose structures are defined primarily by repulsive interactions and shape. Such materials might include photonic crystals with programmed distributions of defects. Optical technology utilizing such materials may offer intriguing solutions to unavoidable heat generation and bandwidth limitations facing the computer industry.

Keywords: non-equilibrium fluids · Foton-M3 · Gradient-driven fluctuations · GRADFLEX
The primary objectives of the GRADFLEX investigation can be summarized as follows:

To investigate non-equilibrium fluctuations in microgravity by studying the behavior of gradient-driven fluctuations in a microgravity environment, where the stabilizing influence of gravity is significantly reduced.
To measure the divergence of large-size fluctuations by observing and quantifying this divergence up to the limits imposed by the sample size.

To quantify the amplitude and spatial extent of fluctuations by precisely measuring the mean-squared amplitude of the fluctuations as a function of both wave vector (spatial extent) and frequency (temporal dynamics).

The investigation aims to rigorously test existing theoretical models of non-equilibrium fluctuations including comparing the measured amplitude and q-dependence of S(q) with predictions, both on Earth and in microgravity.
Beyond the static properties (amplitude and spatial extent), the investigation also seeks to characterize the temporal dynamics of the fluctuations.

In the absence of gravity, thermally-driven fluctuations in a fluid subjected to a temperature gradient will exhibit significantly enhanced amplitude and spatial extent, with their mean-squared amplitude diverging with the size of the fluctuation and exhibiting altered dynamics up to the limits imposed by the sample dimensions.

The GRADFLEX experiment investigated gradient-driven fluctuations in fluids using a dual approach: a 12-day microgravity flight experiment aboard the Foton-M3 satellite and complementary ground-based tests with the same apparatus. Two fluid systems (CS₂ and polystyrene/toluene) were subjected to precisely controlled temperature gradients. Quantitative shadowgraphy, a sensitive optical technique, measured both static (S(q)) and dynamic (S(q,ω)) properties of the fluctuations, with images acquired at specific rates for each. Data analysis involved Fourier transforms and spectral techniques to extract fluctuation amplitudes and dynamics and to address unexpected noise. The core of the study was a rigorous, parameter-free comparison of experimental results with theoretical predictions for both terrestrial and microgravity environments. The approach combined and refined a sophisticated design, enabling robust testing.

Throughout the course of this work it has been necessary to constantly improve the experimental method of choice, namely the quantitative shadowgraph. This development has now reached the stage where it is clear that this method, if handled properly, represents a viable method of carrying out both dynamic and static light scattering at scattering angles so small as to defy the imagination of of anyone who has worked in the field. OASIS studies the unique behavior of liquid crystals in microgravity, including their overall motion and the merging of crystal layers known as smectic islands. Liquid crystals are used for display screens in televisions and clocks, and they also occur in soaps and in cell membranes. The experiment allows detailed studies of the behavior of these structures, and how microgravity affects their unique ability to act like both a liquid and a solid crystal. The specific research objectives are: -To exploit the unique characteristics of freely suspended liquid crystals in a microgravity environment to advance the understanding of fluid state physics. -Study basic 2D hydrodynamics/fluid physics, probe droplet/island diffusion, hydrodynamic interactions, and droplet/island coalescence

In a microgravity environment, freely suspended smectic liquid crystal (FSLC) films will exhibit unique hydrodynamic and interfacial behaviors, such as reduced coarsening rates of island emulsions, enhanced 2D thermocapillarity effects, and distinct equilibrium spatial organization of islands, due to the absence of gravitational forces, convection, and sedimentation, enabling precise tests of theoretical models of 2D hydrodynamics and phase behavior.

The OASIS experiment’s goal is to better understand the unique behavior of liquid crystals in microgravity. OASIS observes the various aspects of liquid crystals behavior in microgravity such as overall fluid motion, diffusion (the movement of particles from an area of high concentration to low concentration) and the merging of liquid crystal film layers called islands, Fundamental studies of complex fluid physics behavior will be accomplished in two dimensional fluids using freely suspended liquid crystals. The impact of the research is to advance the understanding of two-dimensional system physics of complex fluids. Space helmets could use ferroelectric liquid crystal micro-displays. It could advance the understanding of well aligned very high speed electro-optic devices.

Future space helmets may use certain types of liquid crystals in small display screens directly applied to the face shield where astronauts can easily view them. Understanding how liquid crystals behave in microgravity helps researchers to design liquid crystal displays (LCDs) that can perform better in space. Liquid crystals can flow like a liquid, but contain molecules that are arranged in a specific pattern, just like a crystal. Greater understanding of the physics behind these structures could lead to improved liquid crystal display devices, including devices with improved color contrast and response times. It could also advance research in high-speed electro-optic devices used to control a light beam.

Keywords: Microgravity · Diffusion controlled crystal growth · Porosity · MICS · Hydration · Cement Solidification · Density · Cement

The objective of the proposed investigation is to better understand the complex process of cement solidification by conducting experiments in the microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and further the development of an in-situ lunar concrete material.

The research hypothesis for the ISS experiments is that minimizing gravity-driven transport phenomena, such as buoyancy, sedimentation, and convection results in a purely diffusion-controlled hydration process. Without the physical effects induced by gravity, diffusion will lead to a more uniform distribution of phases. As such, the dissolving cement particles will disperse in the aqueous solution, resulting in greater uniformity of features such as pore structures and crystal morphology in the hardened cement matrix. A different microstructure is expected to form in microgravity (µg), which possibly leads to different physical properties of µg-hardened cement paste with respect to that hardened in terrestrial gravity (1g).

Several different mixture combinations of tricalcium aluminate (C3A), tricalcium silicate (C3S), ordinary portland cement (OPC), superplasticizer (SP) and ratios of cement to water were packed in commercially available plastic bags (Burst Pouches®) with separate compartments divided by an internal, burstable seal which allowed mixing of materials under sealed conditions in microgravity and terrestrial conditions. Space and ground samples were mixed simultaneously and at the same conditions of 20 ºC ± 2 ºC, 1 ATM and 35% RH. As such, gravity is considered the only variable between the space and ground experiments. After a specific period of hydration samples were subjected to a wide variety of characterization techniques such as image analysis and mercury intrusion porosimetry (MIP) to assess porosity and pore size distribution, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) to estimate degree of hydration, x-ray diffraction (XRD) for crystalline phase identification, energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) and electron microprobe analysis (EMPA) for compositional analysis. Phase distribution, pore structures, and crystal morphology as a function of composition and gravity level was documented.

The MICS investigation directly addresses the high priority need for lightweight space structures for habitats that protect crew. Results from this investigation enable the characterization of microstructural development in the hardening of cement paste and improve understanding of crystal growth and hydration kinetics, phase formations, pore distribution, and material properties. Also, MICS can increase understanding and control of the crystal growth kinetics, and morphology, to improve concrete properties. Improved cement properties can lead to improved concrete properties, durability, and lower CO2 emissions.

Keywords: Ostwald Ripening · Microgravity · coarsening · kinetics

The primary objective of the microgravity experiment was to measure the temporal evolution of the average size-scale of a solid-liquid mixture during solidification. Specifically, the objective was to measure the average intercept length and the average section area of the solid particles at various times and for various volume fractions of solid. Using this data the amplitude of the temporal power law for the average section area. and intercept length was to be determined. Once the amplitude of the temporal power law is known, the objective is to compare the result to the theoretical predictions on the dependence of the amplitude of the power law on the volume fraction of the coarsening phase. The objective was also to determine the steady-state particle size distribution by measuring the distribution of section area of of the particles in a plane and the intercept length distribution.

The theory of coarsening has been described by Lifshitz, Slyozov and Wagner (LSW) predicts that for the limit of zero volume fraction particles grow with time as the cube root of the average radius, and the particle size distribution becomes independent of time. The investigation hypothesizes that finding a system which satisfies all the constraints of LSW theory such as particles are infinitely separated and there is no diffusional interaction between them is prohibitive for ground-based laboratory condition due to effects of particle sedimentation and buoyancy-induced convection and therefore the theory can only be tested by performing experiments in a microgravity environment.

The sample holder in the Sample Processing Unit (SPU) contained four Lead-Tin samples of 12 mm diameter and 6 mm thickness for various volume fractions of Tin. The SPU heated the samples up to 185 degree C in less than 9.5 min, held the temperature for a predetermined time at 185 ± 0.1 degree C ranging from 0.25 to 48hrs (coarsening phase). The heating system consists of two disc resistance heaters and one ring heater to insure uniform heating with four resistance temperature devices (RTD) installed mid-way between the discs 1 to measure temperature of the samples. Subsequent to the predetermined coarsening time the samples were quenched using pressurized air to nearly room temperature in approximately 1 minute. Once the samples were returned to earth they were sectioned and the measurements of particle size and distribution was performed.

The importance of coarsening from a commercial perspective arises from the major effect that coarsening has on the properties of materials, for example materials can become stronger while undergoing coarsening. The CSLM experiment will assess the validity of the theory of coarsening that has been used to design materials. The result will be a more rational design of materials using a first-principles approach, reduced development cost for the production of new materials and better materials properties. Such a first-principles design of materials will enable NASA and industry to create materials in a rapid cost-efficient manner with the superior properties that are needed for space exploration.

The goal of the BCAT investigations is to further investigate critical, fundamental problems in colloid science and evolve the field of ‘colloid engineering’, which creates materials with novel properties using colloidal particles as precursors. The BCAT-5 investigation had four primary objectives corresponding to specific samples: Phase Seperation (BCAT-5-PhaseSep): to study collapse (phase separation rates that impact product shelf-life). Compete (BCAT-5-Compete): to study the competition between phase separation and crystallization, which is important in the manufacture of plastics and other materials. Seeded Growth (BCAT-5-SeededGrowth): to study the properties of concentrated systems of small particles when 99.8% are identical 0.36 diameter micron spheres and 0.2% are 4.14 microns in diameter (11.5x larger); these seed particles may cause heterogeneous crystal growth. 3D Melt (BCAT-5-3D-Melt): to study the mechanisms of crystal formation and 3D melting using colloidal particles that change size with temperature.

Colloidal particles would exhibit behaviors analogous to atoms, allowing the study of phase transitions, crystallization, and self-organization without the interference of sedimentation and convection present on Earth. This investigation hypothesizes that by taking advantage of microgravity and avoiding sedimentation binary alloys with very different materials and sizes and by addition of polymers particles to induce attractive forces can lead to exciting and promising form of colloidal engineering to synthesize a new class of materials.

BCAT is implemented in a bench-top investigation which is set up on the Maintenance Work Area (MWA) on ISS. The samples are contained within a Fluids Module (FM) which held 10 samples in cuvettes in individual wells. The samples were manually homogenized using a stir bar (a Teflon coated mixing magnet) inside each cuvette. Samples are mixed, examined and imaged using EarthKAM, to document the separation of colloid and liquid components and the formation of colloidal crystals over time.

Insights from BCAT-5 enhance the design of colloidal products critical to space missions, such as food and consumables. The Phase Separation component investigates multi-phase interactions with potential applications in liquid waste recycling, coolant systems, and rocket fuel flow control. By manipulating crystal size during production, BCAT-5 aims to create stronger, more durable materials with extended shelf lives for both terrestrial and extraterrestrial use. Additionally, BCAT-5 advances colloidal engineering by studying how crystallization interacts with phase separation, a key factor in improving consumer and industrial products. Findings help reduce manufacturing defects in colloid-based materials, like plastics, and optimize household goods, such as fabric softeners, by minimizing costly additives. The experiment also supports breakthroughs in next-generation technologies, including advanced optics, medical tools, and smart materials. The Seeded Growth component examines how larger seed particles influence crystal size, enabling better control in producing ceramics, optical filters, and composite materials while refining predictive computer models for crystal formation.

Specific objectives of this investigation were 1. On the ISS and concurrently in earth control experiments, compare incorporation of protein aggregates (monomers versus dimers, trimers, etc.) into growing protein crystals. Detection of aggregates in the crystal will be qualitatively assessed via LMM’s and laboratory fluorescence confocal microscopes and quantitatively measured using mass spectrometry (ion spray and/or MALDI). Keywords: immiscible alloys · Interfacial Stability · Microgravity · hypermonotectic · Coupled Growth

The overall objective of the Coupled Growth in Hypermonotectics is to understand the fundamental physics controlling solidification in immiscible alloy systems. Specific experimental goals were (1) to show that production of an aligned fibrous microstructure is possible in hypermonotectic alloys by achieving interfacial stability and steady state coupled growth through microgravity processing, (2) to determine the influence of alloy composition and growth velocity on microstructure, and (3) to determine the growth velocity and composition range over which interface stability is possible in a hypermonotectic alloy system.

This investigation aimed to answer fundamental unanswered questions concerning solidification of immiscible alloys, namely: (a) is it possible to solidify a hypermonotectic alloy under steady state interfacially stable conditions to produce a fibrous microstructure, (b) can a simple supercooling approach predict stability limits, (c) does extensive diffusion in the liquid phases result in morphological effects not observed in eutectic systems, and (d) what role does surface tension driven flow play at the solidification front.

The CGH experiment investigation flew aboard the Life and Microgravity Spacelab (LMS) mission during the summer of 1996. Processing conditions were controlled in an attempt to force the production of an aligned fibrous phase in the microstructure of processed samples. The Advanced Gradient Heating Facility (AGHF) was used to directionally solidify the immiscible alloys. Aluminum (Al)-Indium (In) alloys were studied and specialized aluminum nitride (AlN) ampoules were used in order to control several undesirable effects that are sometimes observed during low gravity processing. Three alloy compositions, namely 17.3 weight % In monotectic, and 18.5 and 19.7 weight percent In hypermonotectic alloys were processed during this mission. A thermal gradient of 67 C/cm was achieved and all flight samples were processes at a translation velocity of 1 micrometer/s. Ground based control samples were subsequently processed under conditions identical to those of two of the flight samples in order to allow a direct comparison of the results.

Many alloys in immiscible systems show great promise for potential applications in areas that include superconductors, magnetic materials, catalysts, and electrical contacts. For example, some immiscible alloys may be used to produce filters that can remove micron-sized particles for medical applications. Other alloys are expected to exhibit superconducting characteristics or have unusual magnetic properties.

Keywords: Critical Casimir Force · Consolution Curve · polymers · Photon correlation spectroscopy · rheology · Growth kinetics · CCF · Gels · creep · jamming · Gelation

Colloidal stability is critical to soft matter systems, especially to consumer products. These structures change in time, by processes know as coarsening - meaning the spacing between particles compact. This compaction continually changes this structure. When the structures created in the products can longer resist the gravitational stresses (e.g. buoyancy) on the structures, they collapse. The collapse, such as those that occur in geological formations during earthquakes, is often abrupt and without warning (delayed collapse). This is the essence of product instability. For some systems, the gel collapse can be anticipated by precursors, that can potentially be detected and forecasted.

This research will have significant impacts in two areas: • It is not clear how the microscopic structure and its dynamics are related to the gel mechanical properties. The structure evolution controls the aging of the gel, and, on earth, this eventually leads to collapse. This work may significantly enhance the knowledge necessary to advance this important area of science. • Second, relaxation of localized stresses in an amorphous solid brought by a rapid solidification process is ubiquitous in nature and can damage and destroy the materials. Besides affecting the rheological properties of the materials, these dynamics rule the aging of the thermal systems at rest. The detection of failure precursors, as the ones discovered in our colloidal gel, can potentially allow us to forecast the material failure before catastrophic rupture.

ACE-T10 delivered unique insights into the restructuring behavior of thermo-reversible colloidal gels, a topic of noticeable interest for the community of scientists dealing with soft materials. In normal gravity experiments, the ACE-T10 science team found evidence that the aging of these soft gels proceed via a sequence of sudden intermittent bursts of dynamical activity that resembles the ‘critical avalanche’ phenomena observed in several driven systems. The evidence collected suggests that, in a soft solid, these avalanches may be triggered by thermal agitation and occur spontaneously, even in the absence of other external forces. However, because of the density difference between the fluid and the particles in the gel network, gravity may play a role as well. Performing the ACE-T10 experiment in microgravity provided a unique opportunity to determine the gravity contribution.

The ACE-T10 experiment exploited the Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) and the Light Microscopy Module (LMM). The Light Microscopy Module (LMM) is an automated microscope. It permitted flexible imaging (e.g., bright field, dark field, phase contrast, confocal microscopy) for physics experiments and can be controlled remotely from the ground. The LMM accommodated sample change-out and fluid containment and included a glove box for on-orbit sample manipulation.

The ACE-T10 experiment used include confocal microscopy, which utilized a 532-nm frequency-doubled Nd:YAG laser, a confocal scanner, and an 8- to 12-bit digital CCD camera. The scanner captured 30 frames per second of confocal images by the CCD camera. A sample’s three-dimensional crystal structure can thus be reconstructed by assembling individual slices with an image analysis program. This information, in turn, enabled the observation and measurement of the colloidal growth, structure, and dynamics. The confocal module was attached and aligned to the side of the LMM. The microscope used a reflecting mirror to direct the light to and from the sample.

ACE-T10 utilized 6 capillary cells in 2 holding modules. The capillary cells, each contained about 20 microliters of the sample fluid and a magnetic stainless steel stir bar. Samples were stirred prior to example. The sample temperature was adjusted between 20 – 60 °C in order to find the transition temperature where the sample became a gel.

Earth benefits/spin-off applications include understanding the behavior of weak gels and their aging can help materials scientists to make consumer product with longer shelf lives. In addition, because several features of the failure dynamics of disordered materials are system independent, the results obtained using this model colloidal system can be generalized to other materials. This potentially can help to develop new way to characterize aging material and suggest their replacement before catastrophic failure.

The objective of this experiment is the investigation of the assembly of complex structures from micron-scale colloidal particles interacting via tunable attractive interactions. Regulating temperature enables control of particle interactions.

This simple reversible process is controlled by adjusting the size of the tunable temperature fluctuations in a two-component fluid (solvent). In principle, the ingredients are simple: particles suspended in a binary solvent, without the addition of any other components.

By studying this process based on critical Casimir forces in microgravity, where sedimentation and convection are essentially removed, we will learn how to adjust complex attractive particle interactions. This simple reversible process is controlled by adjusting the size of the tunable temperature fluctuations in a two-component fluid (solvent). In principle, the ingredients are simple: particles suspended in a binary solvent, without the addition of any other components.

Understanding self-assembly processes like the critical Casimir effect will teach ways to grow complex nanostructured materials. Furthermore, these experiments will provide fundamental insight into the nature of temperature-controlled super structure assembly, the relation between complex interactions and complex equilibrium and non-equilibrium structures, and the dynamics of both equilibrium and non-equilibrium growth processes.
The critical Casimir effect is affected by temperature, particle size and relative concentrations and will impact the growth of complex nanostructured materials.

The TEMPUS (Tiegelfreies ElektroMagnetisches Prozessieren Unter Schwerelosgkeit) facility is a research instrument designed to perform electromagnetic levitation studies in reduced gravity. TEMPUS was a joint undertaking between DARA, the German space agency, and the Microgravity Science and Applications Division of NASA. Specific objectives for the different investigations carried out by US Principal Investigators using this facility is categorized by different classes: Class A: Studies of undercooling phenomena and the kinetics of nucleation (Prof. M. Flemings, MIT, Prof. R. Bayuzick, Vanderbilt Univ), Class B: Measurement of specific heat in liquid metals using an AC calorimetry technique (Prof W. Johnson, CALTECH), Class C: Measurement of viscosity and surface tension of undercooled metals (Prof. J. Szkeley, Prof. M. Flemings, MIT), Class D: Measurement of thermal expansion in undercooled materials (Prof W. Johnson, CALTECH). In addition to the US Principal Investigators, available data from European investigations performed on TEMPUS and captured here include Viscosity and Surface Tension of Undercooled Metallic Melts (Dr. Egry, DLR, Germany), Thermophysical Properties of Unde

Levitation, positioning and processing of materials which are not in direct contact with container surfaces, provides a unique opportunity to study a number of phenomena. In particular, the lack of contact with container walls reduces the possibility for heterogeneous nucleation in studies of the processing of molten materials. The study of the properties and solidification of undercooled materials is facilitated by containerless processing.

Metallic samples of 7 or 8 mm diameter are positioned in the TEMPUS coils by electromagnetic forces and melted by induced currents. A ''squeezing'' force is then applied to a stably positioned liquid sample to induce oscillations. The rate of decay of the amplitude of these oscillations can be observed in order to measure the viscosity at different temperatures, while the frequency of the oscillation modes is used to deduce the surface tension at these temperatures. Measurements are planned on reactive, refractory melts (Zr), high-viscosity eutectics (ZrNi, PdSi), and industrial alloys (Fe-Cr-Ni) in addition to standard materials for comparison (Au, Ni). In addition, mathematical modeling designed to give a detailed understanding of what can be expected from prevailing conditions in the flight experiments was also developed.

The accurate determination of the thermophysical properties of liquid materials is important for fundamental and practical reasons, including verification of atomistic models of the liquid state, nucleation studies of phase transition, and modeling of materials processing operations. In addition, these studies often focus on advanced materials such as metallic glass forming materials. Metallic glasses are an industrially important new class of materials. They are ductile, isotropic and corrosion resistant and are used in magnetic storage media films.

The objective of the proposed investigation is to better understand how the intensity of convection and the direction of the flow influences the evolution of the mushy zone, macro- and micro-segregation, morphology of dendrites, the growth mode and spatial arrangement of intermetallic precipitates.

Dendritic metrics of the directionally solidified (DS) samples are expected to have dendritic characteristics that compare very well to model predictions for growth in the absence of convection. Earth-grown samples are not anticipated to compare well, indicating that the convection in Earth grown alloys does indeed play a role in microstructural development during the solidification process. Further, Earth-grown samples exhibit a type of macrosegregation called ''steepling” in which the periphery of a DS-ed sample is of eutectic composition and is seen in alloys with solutes that increase the density of the liquid during solidification. Samples grown aboard the ISS are not expected to have steepling.

3 different Al-Si alloys were directionally solidified under different thermal gradient and furnace translation velocities. Along with micro and macro-segregation, dendritic characteristics including primary arm spacing and trunk diameters were quantified. Microgravity results were compared to those obtained under terrestrial conditions. A finite volume modeling approach was undertaken in the absence of convection and predictions were compared to data obtained from microgravity and terrestrial samples.

The research is relevant to a process known as directional solidification, which is used for producing critical castings that are used in gas turbine engines. Gas turbine engines power aircraft (i.e., often called ''jet engines'') and are also used to generate electric power. These castings are made of vacuum melted alloys that are capable of withstanding the demanding conditions at high temperatures and consequently the metallurgical structure of the alloys must be of the highest quality. The research is leading to an improved understanding of how microstructures and segregation form in directionally solidified castings; hence the science of producing such castings will be enhanced as a result of the research. In addition, the research findings relate to many other types of castings, including billets and ingots, of alloys (i.e., steel, aluminum alloys, etc.) that are critical for metal fabrication. In addition, the benchmark microgravity data allows validation of models predicting dendritic metrics such as primary and secondary arm spacing and trunk diameter. Such validated simulation models can enable optimization of casting parameters.

The primary scientific goal of the proposed terrestrial and planned microgravity molten metal capillary flow experiments is to better understand the physics of the flow of molten metals over the topographically modified surfaces (e.g., filling in the holes, flow over sharp edges and/or flow over surfaces having variable curvatures). By performing capillary flow tests both on Earth and in a microgravity environment, the effects of microgravity on the kinetics of the larger masses of melt flow, and ultimate equilibrium shape of the meniscus will be closely examined. The objective of the microgravity experiments is to provide benchmark data against which theoretical models and computer simulations can be tested. The BRAINS project’s primary pragmatic/engineering obective is that a capillary flow of braze under microgravity conditions would enable a repair or bonding of larger and/or more irregular mating surfaces defects, compared to the terrestrial conditions. This would be important for future development of advanced brazing techniques with applications to both damage repair and construction in space.

A series of space (ISS) and terrestrial experiments, integrated with modeling and analysis are expected to answer the following practical and fundamental questions: (1) How can the absence of gravity and dominance of capillary forces be take advantage of in transporting the molten braze? (2) Which brazing alloy and the brazing technique will enable strong and efficient bonding of selected proxies of structural elements and facilitate a repair. That is, can brazing be done in space and/or on board of space vehicles by using flux-less braze? Specifically: A comparison between flux and flux-less brazing under space and terrestrial conditions can answer underlying scientific questions related to molten metal flow kinetics, specifically wetting and spreading of liquid clad/filler over topographically modified surfaces.

Before being assembled into the ampoule, the samples were always ultrasonically cleaned in the sequence of (i) soapy water, (ii) water, (iii) 190 proof ethanol, and then dried in air or a compressed air. A double nitrogen purge was done before sealing the ampoule. Three configurations of the Al alloy filler and corresponding substrates were considered as relevant for the intended study: (i) HOLE, (ii) PIN and (iii) Hollow Pin. Solidification Using a Baffle in Sealed Ampoules” (SUBSA) furnace, which was designed for operation in the ISS’s Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) was used for this investigation. All samples were placed in the isothermal region of the furnace instrumented with thermocouples. The furnace was heated to the dwell temperature (600 - 605 °C ± 2K) at a rate of 5 K/minute (optimal 10K/minute). A dwell time was maintained for completion of capillary flow and establishing of the equilibrium meniscus shape. Subsequent cooling of the samples was performed at the maximum cooling rate allowed by the facility. Capillary topography identification and microstructure evaluation was performed on all samples.

A brazing process may be used to mitigate the consequences of high velocity micro meteoroids’ and/or space debris’ impacts, and possible catastrophic penetration of aluminum man-made objects in space. Second, construction in space would necessitate joining complex assemblies, e.g., habitat systems, with brazing being one meaningful manufacturing option of permanent bonding. Validation fundamental models including phase field models will allow prediction of terrestrial brazing quality.
