Keywords: crystalline systems · PK-3+ · ESA · Physics · Complex plasmas · PKE-Nefedov · Plasma Crystals · Plasma

Plasma crystals are a new kind of matter, rediscovered in 1994. They form under certain conditions in a complex (dusty) plasma. There, the electrically charged dust particles arrange in a regular macroscopic crystal lattice. This structure allows for an investigation of the properties of condensed matter on the kinetic level. This means that basic processes, such as melting, can be followed by observing the motion of individual particles. PK-3 will give investigators a better understanding of plasma in space and will determine the critical points for the plasma.

Gravity plays an important role for the structure of plasma crystals. In microgravity large 3-dimensional plasma crystals can be grown and studied in detail on the most fundamental, the kinetic level. Complex plasmas can be seen as model systems for the investigation of fundamental phenomena in liquids and crystals and provide information on the motion of single particles (“atoms”). This provides new insights into the field of condensed matter.

PK-3 Plus is a symmetrical driven radio-frequency plasma discharge with special features for the investigation of complex plasmas under microgravity conditions. As a second generation laboratory, PK-3 Plus provides major new possibilities for these investigations due to its design improvements relative to the first long-term experiment PKE-Nefedov. The PK-3 Plus apparatus allows investigations at neutral gas pressures between 0.05 - 2.5 millibar and radio frequency (rf) power of 0.01 - 1 W. The complex plasma can consist of monodisperse particles in a size range from 1 - 20 micrometers. Up to six particle sizes can be added to the experimental volume. It is possible to change the number of particles, the composition of particles, the plasma conditions and the neutral gas pressure during one experiment. The particle cloud can be excited by an electrical low frequency signal on the electrodes (0.1 - 100 Hz at a maximum amplitude of 50 V) or by a low frequency modulation of the rf-amplitude in different wave forms (sinusoidal, square, pulse, etc.).

The PK-3 Plus investigation has two major pieces of equipment: the experimental block, and the telescience system (TS). The research will be performed on the ISS inside the plasma chamber situated inside of the experimental block. The experimental block is attached via a tube to the space environment to produce the prevacuum for turbomolecular pump, which can produce pressure in the plasma chamber less than 10-5 millibar.

The TS is the computer in which the chamber conditions can be altered via actuators in the experimental block and the storage unit for the data collected. This PK3 Plus laboratory has state of the art hardware and software, and provides better diagnostics than previous hardware. The PK-3 Plus laboratory was operated on the Russian segment of ISS by Russian cosmonauts mostly.

Typical experimental campaigns have 3 or 4 runs to meet the requirements of the investigator. There are two modes, automatic and manual, for this investigation. During the manual mode, crew time will be required to complete the investigation. Experimenters are following live video transmission from the experimental block in the control center in Korolev guiding the cosmonaut via audio contact for experiment parameters optimization. Full set Recorded videos and housekeeping data are to be returned on hard drives via Soyuz capsule.

The experiments run on three or four consecutive days during single experimental campaign. Some days areon automatic, as mentioned above, and some days are manual operations, depending on the cosmonaut availability and investigators plans. On automatic days, the machine can be left alone to run, passively taking measurements of the complex plasma behaviors under microgravity. On the manual day, there will be a cosmonaut present, adjusting settings to achieve the required states of the plasma. The experiment is expected to take approximately 90 minutes each day.

99% of the visible matter in the universe is in the plasma state and dust is ubiquitous, too. Thus so called dusty plasmas can be found in interstellar media, in planetary forming discs, in cometary atmospheres, in Saturn rings, etc. The results from the PK-3 Plus laboratory on the ISS on the charging of the microparticles/dust and their interaction with each other and the surrounding plasma, the so-called basic fundamental questions, are very helpful in the understanding of dusty plasmas in space. Additionally, complex plasmas are models for liquid and crystalline systems providing new insights into the formation and behavior of condensed matter.

The primary objectives of this investigation are: 1. Use molecular biology to produce closely related protein constructs that display differences in growth rate dispersion during crystallization. Measure the intermolecular ‘attractiveness’ of each construct, then model the inter-particle forces, diffusion and convection. 2. Measure and compare the growth rate dispersion of ground and microgravity grown crystals. Growth rate dispersion will be measured for ground control crystals using routine crystallization apparatus. In addition, growth rate dispersion will be measure for ground and microgravity grown crystals using the flight apparatus. 3. Characterize the quality of both ground and microgravity grown crystals. Sophisticated X-ray analysis along with X-ray structural data collection will be used to quantify and characterize crystal quality. 4. Link the knowledge about inter-particle forces, measured acceleration levels, calculated flow rates and the resultant X-ray analysis to develop a model and predictive ground-based tests to identify those samples producing crystals on the ground that would be improved in microgravity.

Removing or greatly reducing the effects of buoyancy-driven convection and sedimentation in microgravity will result in slower, diffusion-controlled molecular transport that can yield larger crystals with fewer defects. It is postulated that growth rate dispersion is reduced in microgravity due to the diffusive rather than convective flow regime that delivers macromolecules to the crystal. Based on previous experimental observations it is hypothesized that the presence of growth rate dispersion in macromolecular crystals grown on the ground is an indicator of crystals that can be improved when grown in microgravity.

Several cassettes were identically configured containing three samples, one set in capillaries 1-6, another sample in capillaries 7-12, and the third in capillaries 13-18. The capillaries were loaded so that capillaries 1-6 contained theWT* construct, capillaries 7-12 the S44E WT* construct and finally, capillaries 13-18 the S44F WT* construct. This investigation uses ground and microgravity-based observations to predict which proteins would benefit from crystallization in microgravity, improving the information that may be obtained from them.

Long-duration protein crystal growth experiments on the ISS with photo documentation, and subsequent analysis of the comparisons between 1g and μg crystals, will enable a more complete understanding of why proteins and other macromolecules often form more perfect crystals in microgravity than they do on earth. If it could be predicted which macromolecular samples could be improved by crystal growth in microgravity, then the true potential of this medium could be exploited in an efficient manner. Structural biology of protein-protein complexes and integral membrane proteins are currently a high NIH priority due to their importance for systems biology, disease mechanisms and structure-guided drug development. It is hypothesized that fluctuating hydrodynamics will dominate domain growth at low volume fractions, challenging classical theories. A sharp transition between growth regimes is expected. Mechanical quenches are hypothesized to be a viable method for inducing phase ordering. The vapor recoil force is believed to significantly influence bubble dynamics and wetting near the critical point. Adiabatic volume changes are expected to reveal the dynamics of the Piston Effect. Critical water is hypothesized to follow the same universality class, and external vibration will affect the dynamics.

The investigation approach for DECLIC-ALI centers on conducting experiments within the microgravity environment of the ISS, utilizing the DECLIC facility and its specialized Alice-Like Insert (ALI, ALI-R, and ALI-2). The approach involves precise control of the temperature and density of the SF6 sample, including temperature and mechanical quenches, as well as heat pulse techniques. A suite of optical diagnostics (Interferometry, shadowgraphy, light scattering, and direct observation) is used to visualize and quantify the SF6 fluid behavior. Different sample cell configurations, including fixed and variable volume cells, are employed within the ALI insert. Data acquisition is performed at high frequencies, and the data are analyzed quantitatively, with a strong emphasis on comparing experimental results with theoretical predictions. The overall approach is iterative, building upon previous space-based experiments and refining both experimental techniques and theoretical models, all focused on understanding the critical phenomena of SF6.

The DECLIC facility provides power, communications, command, control, data storage, and multiple, flexible optical capabilities in support of each experiment. The knowledge gained will assist in the understanding of the behavior of cryogenic (of or relating to very low temperatures) rocket propellants for the study of dynamics regarding near-ambient temperature critical fluids. DECLIC is designed for telescience from the ground and will offer scientists the capability to remotely control experiment conditions onboard the ISS provided by DECLIC lockers. The use of near-critical fluids allows important parameters (e.g., compressibility of supercritical fluids, density of gas and liquid phases, surface tension) to be easily varied in a scaled way by using small changes in temperature. The investigation aims to characterize and quantify critical flow dynamics in open capillary channels of parallel plate and groove geometries. A primary objective is determining the critical flow rates at which free surface destabilization (''choking'') and gas ingestion occur, emphasizing the capillary-inertial regime. The investigation will examine the relationship between critical flow rate and channel length for complete and half-channel configurations. Controlled, low-frequency flow oscillations will be introduced to probe instability onset sensitivity across geometries and lengths. High-fidelity data on free surface shapes and critical velocities will be acquired to validate theoretical models and assess underlying assumptions, refining predictive capabilities for capillary flows relevant to spacecraft fluid management.

The primary hypothesis guiding CCF-CV EU1 is that a limiting flow rate, or 'choking' phenomenon, exists in open capillary channels with parallel plate and groove geometries. A relationship between the fluid velocity, the channel geometry, and the fluid properties governs this limit. Furthermore, it is hypothesized that the introduction of wave oscillations within the flow will impact the critical flow rate, with the amplitude and frequency of these oscillations playing a significant role in the flow behavior and the onset of choking.

The program described here seeks to improve the understanding of the fundamental mechanisms that constitute nucleate pool boiling. The vehicle for accomplishing this is an investigation, including experiments to be conducted in microgravity and coupled with appropriate analyses, of the heat transfer and vapor bubble dynamics associated with nucleation, bubble growth or collapse, and subsequent motion. Certain effects that can be neglected at normal Earth gravity, such as surface tension and vapor momentum, can become quite significant in microgravity. Momentum imparted to the liquid by the vapor bubble during growth tends to draw the vapor bubble away from the surface, depending on the rate of growth, which in turn is governed by the temperature distribution in the liquid. Thermophoretic forces, arising from the variation of the liquid-vapor surface tension with temperature, on the other hand, tend to move the vapor bubble toward the region of higher temperature. The bubble motion will be governed by which of these two effects prevail.

The elements of nucleate boiling, for which research conducted under microgravity would advance the basic understanding, are: 1. Nucleation or onset of boiling. Indications are that both heater surface temperature and temperature distribution in the liquid are necessary to describe nucleation. 2. The dynamic growth of a vapor bubble in the vicinity of the heater surface. This includes the shape as well as motion of the liquid-vapor interface as growth is taking place. These are influenced by the liquid temperature distribution at the initiation of growth. 3. The subsequent behavior of the vapor bubble. This includes the motion, whether departure takes place or not, and the associated heat transfer.

The approach encompasses a comprehensive experimental methodology designed to dissect the nuances of the boiling process in an environment where gravity's influence is minimal. This approach aims to isolate and analyze the core mechanisms that drive nucleate pool boiling, offering insights that are obscured under normal Earth gravity conditions.

Here is an outline of the investigation's methodological approach: 1. Experimental Setup in Microgravity: a. The investigation utilizes a specially designed experimental apparatus capable of accurately controlling and measuring heat flux, liquid subcooling levels, and temperature distribution within the liquid and at the heater surface. This apparatus is deployed in a microgravity environment provided by space-based platforms to ensure the minimization of gravity's influence on the boiling process.

2. Controlled Heat Flux Application: a. A key component of the approach involves applying a controlled heat flux to a pool of liquid, initiating the boiling process. The heat flux is carefully modulated to explore a range of boiling conditions, from gentle nucleation to vigorous boiling, under varying levels of liquid subcooling.

3. High-Resolution Data Acquisition: a. To capture the dynamics of bubble formation, growth, and departure, the investigation employs high-resolution, high-speed imaging techniques, along with precise temperature and heat flux measurement tools. This data acquisition setup allows for the detailed observation and analysis of bubble behavior and heat transfer phenomena during the boiling process.

4. Parameter Variation: a. The investigation systematically varies key parameters, including the heat flux magnitude, the degree of liquid subcooling, and the pressure within the system, to study their effects on the nucleation process, bubble dynamics, and heat transfer rates. This parameter variation helps in identifying the critical factors that influence nucleate pool boiling under microgravity.

5. Data Analysis and Model Development: a. The collected data undergoes rigorous analysis to elucidate the fundamental mechanisms of nucleate pool boiling, focusing on nucleation criteria, bubble growth rates, and heat transfer characteristics. Insights gained from the analysis are used to develop and refine predictive models that can accurately describe boiling behavior under a variety of conditions.

6. Cross-Comparison with Earth Gravity Data: a. Findings from the microgravity experiments are compared with data obtained from similar experiments conducted under Earth gravity conditions. This cross-comparison aids in isolating the effects of gravity on the boiling process and contributes to the development of generalized models that can predict boiling behavior across different gravitational environments.

The primary objective of the proposed study is to develop a mechanistic model for nucleate boiling under microgravity conditions. Specific objectives included:
Single bubble dynamics (nucleation, growth, and departure) under microgravity conditions under constant wall temperature.
Effect of liquid subcooling, wall superheat, and system pressure on single bubble dynamics.
Heat flux variation on the heated surface during single bubble evolution.
Lateral merger of bubbles formed at neighboring sites and mechanism of vapor removal from the surface.

In microgravity conditions, where buoyancy forces become negligible, it is expected that forces arising from the inertia of the liquid, evaporation, and condensation at the vapor-liquid interface, disjoining pressure, capillary pressure gradient, and the resulting flow field will become more dominant. The study aimed to understand and quantify the effect of these forces and identify the conditions under which quasi-static or steady-state boiling is possible under prolonged microgravity duration.

The research utilized a systematic and comprehensive approach to understand the complexities of nucleate pool boiling in a microgravity environment. The approach was characterized by a strategic ''building block'' strategy, progressing from simpler to more complex scenarios, enabling a gradual and insightful understanding of the underlying physics.
Here's a detailed breakdown of the investigation approach:

The research commenced by focusing on the behavior of a single bubble nucleating from a pre-fabricated cavity on the aluminum wafer. This fundamental building block allowed for a detailed examination of bubble growth, departure (if any), and the associated heat transfer processes in microgravity conditions.

Building upon the knowledge gained from single bubble studies, the investigation then explored the interactions of multiple bubbles. Experiments were conducted to study the merger of bubbles nucleating from different cavities. This stage investigated how bubbles merge in the lateral direction, the mechanisms of vapor removal from the heated surface after merger, and the impact of these interactions on the overall heat transfer rates.

The investigation then broadened its scope by conducting experiments with boiling occurring over the entire heater surface. This aimed to obtain the boiling curve, which depicts the relationship between heat flux and wall superheat, under microgravity conditions. This provided a macroscopic view of nucleate pool boiling, considering the collective behavior of numerous bubbles.

The experimental work was tightly coupled with complete numerical simulations of the boiling process. These simulations employed advanced computational fluid dynamics (CFD) techniques to capture the intricate details of bubble dynamics and heat transfer. The simulations accounted for a range of factors including time-varying system pressure and temperatures, the presence of dissolved gas in the liquid, surface tension effects, and the influence of microlayer evaporation. The numerical model was rigorously validated against the experimental data obtained in the NPBX experiments.

The ultimate goal of the research was to develop a mechanistic model for nucleate pool boiling heat transfer under microgravity conditions. This model, based on the physical understanding derived from experimental observations and validated numerical simulations, aimed to provide a reliable tool for predicting boiling behavior across a wide range of parameters and conditions relevant to space applications.

While the primary motivation for this investigation was to advance our understanding of boiling heat transfer in the context of space applications, the knowledge gained has significant implications for Earth-based technologies and scientific understanding as well.
Here are some key potential impacts and benefits:
1. Improved Understanding of Boiling at Earth Gravity:

By studying boiling in a microgravity environment where buoyancy forces are negligible, researchers can gain a clearer understanding of the interplay of other forces and phenomena that influence boiling behavior. This knowledge can, in turn, enhance our comprehension of boiling processes under Earth's gravity, where buoyancy often masks the effects of these more subtle factors.
2. Development of More Efficient Heat Transfer Systems:

The insights gained from this research can contribute to the development of more efficient boiling heat transfer systems for a wide range of applications on Earth. Enhanced efficiency translates to reduced energy consumption, lower operational costs, and a reduced environmental footprint.

As electronic devices continue to shrink in size, effective thermal management becomes increasingly critical. Understanding boiling in microgravity is crucial for developing innovative cooling solutions for miniaturized electronics, as these devices often operate at high heat fluxes and face challenges in dissipating heat effectively.

This research offers valuable insights into fundamental fluid physics phenomena, including the behavior of bubbles, interfacial phenomena, and the dynamics of multiphase flows. This knowledge can lead to advancements in diverse fields, such as materials science, biomedical engineering, and environmental science.

The heater power was then turned down to maintain the desired isothermal hold. Surface excitation was conducted using varying volage from the electrodes at this temperature. docs.title: Plasma Kristall 4
passages: Research area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter
Hardware: European Physiology Module (EPM) PK-4 Facility
Keywords: Soft Matter · Complex Plasmas · Thermodynamics · Plasma Physics · Statistical Physics

PK-4 is not an apparatus dedicated for specific experiments but rather a laboratory which shall offer the possibility to perform a large variety of experiments with complex plasmas and to react to new developments in this field in a manner as flexible as possible. The main interest lies in the investigation of the liquid phase and flow phenomena of complex plasmas for which PK-4 is especially suited thanks to a DC-discharge and its geometry (elongated glass tube with a large observational access).

The experiments for PK-4 can be divided into research in three classes of fundamental questions: 1. Microscopic properties of complex plasmas This category comprises the charging of the particles, the external forces on the particles (e.g. ion drag), the fundamental interactions between the particles, agglomeration, and particle growth. 2. Macroscopic properties of complex plasmas In this category belong hydrodynamics (e.g. viscosity), thermodynamics (e.g. equation of state), and non-equilibriums aspects (e.g. lane formation, self-organisation) of complex plasmas. 3. Generic properties of classical many-body systems Complex plasmas are ideal model systems for studying various problems of strongly coupled many-body systems in solid state physics, fluid physics, plasma physics, nano-technology and even nuclear physics because complex plasmas can easily be produced and observed in real time on the microscopic and kinetic level. Hence dynamical processes can be investigated on the level of single particles which is not possible in most systems.

Therefore new insights in the dynamics of those processes can be provided. Typical examples are crystallization and melting, phonons in plasma crystals, dust waves, Mach cones, nozzles, turbulence, and nano-fluidics.

The basic experimental protocol starts with an evacuation of the plasma chamber for several hours (a minimum of 20 hours; base pressure: less than 10-3 Pa) to guarantee good plasma conditions, e.g. no striations.
Then neon or argon gas is filled in with a gas flow of typically 2 sccm reaching pressures between 5 and 250 Pa.
Afterwards the plasma is ignited by the high-voltage (about 1000 V) of the DC electrodes corresponding to a DC current of the order of 1 mA and a longitudinal electric field of about 2 V/cm.
Then the micro-particles are injected. They get quickly charged in the plasma and drift from the cathode to the anode with a typical velocity between 1 and 10 cm/s.
In addition, the electric fields from the two RF coils/electrodes or the fast polarity switching can be used to manipulate the particles, e.g. to capture and confine them.

Gas flow, modulation of the DC and RF fields, the powerful manipulation laser, the thermal manipulator, and the EM electrode can also be used to manipulate the particles, e.g. to accelerate them or to introduce oscillations.

A sketch of the PK-4 experiment is shown in Figure 1. The micro-particles are made visible by illumination with a laser beam, which is widened into a sheet by a cylindrical lens. The scattered light is recorded by one or two CCD cameras (e.g. up to 200 frames per second, with a maximum resolution of about e.g.10 microns/pixel). The light emission (“plasma glow”) from the plasma will be measured using the narrow band IF-filters.

The basic measurements comprise the positions of the particles, their velocities (extracted from the track length of the particles or from their positions in consecutive images), and correlations between the particles. These quantities are determined from the images by using a dedicated IDL program or other methods for image analysis.
At the end of each experiment run the particles will be removed by gas flow before the plasma is switched off in order to avoid the contamination of the glass walls

PK-4 enables fundamental investigation of flows and related instabilities, by mimicking molecular mechanisms at a scale which allows for real time in-situ optical observations. This requires on-orbit experiments to be undertaken in order to observe the processes at work, which are obviously disturbed by the influence of gravity on Earth. Even though PK-4 is principally a fundamental experiment, understanding the processes at work and understanding how complex plasmas can be influenced by varying research parameters gives a better understanding of how improvements can be made in areas and industries where plasmas are used. Understanding how dusty plasmas behave in microgravity could shed light on plasma phenomena in space, which could lead to new research methods or improved spacecraft designs.

passages: PSI-97 · RSD-AFF — Ring-Sheared Drop - Amyloid Fibril Formation

Keywords: RSD · Shear-induced fibrillation · Fluid Dynamic Modeling · Biotechnology · Amyloid Fibril Formation · Protein Crystallization · Interfacial Shear · Proteins

This campaign centered on four main objectives: (i) engineering the RSD to flight proven hardware, (ii) testing measurement and instrumentation methods aboard the ISS, (iii) studying protein kinetics under interfacial shear, and (iv) measuring and modeling protein solution rheology.

The primary obective of this investigation is to quantify the effects of flow on fibrillization in the bulk and at interfaces, specifically at the air/water interface. This includes studying protein kinetics under interfacial shear, and measuring and modeling protein solution rheology. The overall objective is project to advance the mechanistic description of fibrillization by determining how shearing flow affects each of the stages of amyloid formation process − protein unfolding and nuclei formation, growth into protofibrils, and elongation and intertwining into mature fibrils and fibril growth − without any influence from solid boundaries.

The absence of gravity in a microgravity environment will significantly alter the amyloid fibril formation process in proteins.The hypothesis tested was that if protein solutions in microgravity are seeded with fibrils and subject to steady interfacial shear, then amyloidogenesis will occur with the extent of gelation depending on total protein concentration.

The Ring Shear Drop (RSD) is used to facilitate amyloidogenesis and study flow dynamics without solid wall interactions. It uses surface tension to contain fluids in a microgravity environment. Techniques like Particle Tracking Velocimetry (PTV) are used to measure fluid dynamics and protein interactions. This information was used to create high-fidelity computational models. Formation and flow of protein aggregates on the surface of the drop will be imaged by the microscope as a function of time. The RSD imaged the surface of a 2.50 cm diameter drop of protein solution with shear imposed by the rotation of one of the two sharp-edged rings (essentially knife edges) that constrain the drop. A separate measure of the turbidity quantified by the extinction of a light beam through the center of the drop provided an independent signal for fibril formation. A variable degree of shear was imposed on the drop with a negligible contact with solid boundaries. Velocity of the fluid on the surface of the drop will be determined by standard cross-correlation techniques from images obtained by the microscope. Details regarding sample composition and experimental parameters can be found in RSD Ex

Amyloid fibril formation in proteins is of great interest because of its role in diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. For example, the waxy plaque choking off neurons in Alzheimer’s patients consists of the A-beta protein that has formed into amyloid fibrils. The microgravity environment aboard the ISS was utilized to study the biophysics of protein amyloidogenesis. The absence of gravity allows surface tension to provide fluid containment so that wall nucleation and other complications associated with solid containers can be avoided. Flow effects on protein fibrillization was studied at fluid interfaces similar to physiological processes, as all brain tissue consists of interfaces with fluidity, being comprised of cell membranes. The goal is to advance mechanistic descriptions of amyloid fibril formation.

The major scientific objectives of this investigation were as follows: · to enhance the fundamental understanding of dynamics of insoluble particles at the solid-liquid interface; · to obtain experimental data for the critical velocity of particle engulfment in a convection-free environment; · to validate present theoretical models; · to improve the understanding of physics associated with solidification of liquid metals - ceramic particles mixtures; · to investigate aspects of melt processing of particulate metal matrix composites in the unique microgravity environment which will yield some vital information for terrestrial applications; · to further develop the elements of the numerical model into a comprehensive model that takes into account convection effects.

During solidification of metal-insoluble particles systems the particles interact with the solidification front. The solutal and thermal field, as well as fluid motion at the solid-liquid interface (SLI) will influence both interface morphology and the particle/interface interaction itself. This investigation hypothesizes that based on the nature of interaction and balance of forces acting on the particle there is a critical SLI velocity below which particles are pushed ahead of the advancing interface, and above which particle engulfment occurs. For planar SLI the critical velocity results from the forces acting on the particle. These forces include particle-SLI interaction force, drag force on the particle, gravitational force, Saffman force, and Magnus force. The last three are strongly affected by the level of gravitational acceleration.

The experimental approach was to perform directional solidification experiments with a pure metal, aluminum, doped with low volume fraction of insoluble particles, ZrO2. These experiments were carried out during the Life and Microgravity Science (LMS) mission on board the space shuttle Columbia. In addition, transparent organic matrices such as succinonitrile and biphenyl doped with polystryrene particles or glass beads were used to observe the interaction between the particle and solidification interface in real time. The experiments with the organic matrices were performed during the United States Microgravity Payload 4 (USMP-4) mission also on board the space shuttle Columbia. Planar interfaces were produced through appropriate manipulation of the solidification variables, so that a clear pushing/engulfment transition (PET) of the particles could be determined. Both ground and microgravity experiments were conducted. Recognizing that the interaction between the particle and the solidification front is not completely a steady state process, a dynamic non-steady-state model was developed based on the fact that a particle, initially at rest, must have an accelerated motion in order

A fundamental understanding of the phenomena associated with particle/interface interaction during solidification will permit the development of novel techniques for processing of particulate metal matrix composites through melting and solidification. Similar concepts apply to inclusion management in casting alloys. As for most other metallurgical applications it is desired to avoid inclusion segregation at grain boundaries. Results of this research can be extrapolated straightforward to “clean steel” technology. Another interesting application of particle pushing is in the processing of single crystals ceramic where strong flux pinning particles are desired to be homogeneously incorporated in the superconducting crystal. Insights from this investigation can also be applied to the field of cryobiology where the study of the interaction of cells (yeast cells, red blood cells) with ice crystals when freezing aqueous solutions makes it possible to investigate the mechanism of the mechanical destruction of biological structures by ice crystals on freezing biological materials. The objective of this investigation was to obtain benchmark data on cellular and dendritic growth under diffusive growth conditions. Precise measurements of interface shape, cell/dendrite tip radius, tip composition and tip temperature will be carried out as a function of composition, growth rate and thermal gradient values. By systematically varying the process parameters in the absence of gravity-induced convection, the range of interface morphologies will be obtained, yielding insight into the underlying principles that govern dynamical pattern selection. Directional solidification experiments conducted in microgravity using transparent organic analogues will provide real time benchmark data to quantitatively determine conditions for the planar to cellular and cell to dendrite transitions and validate a predictive phase field 3D being developed as part of the investigation.

When a planar solid-liquid becomes unstable, under certain growth conditions, complex interactions among perturbed regions can lead to different amplification rates of different wavelengths that determines the final selection of the reorganized pattern. This complex dynamical process selects a small range of wavelengths, from an unstable spectrum of wavelengths, to form a periodic array of cells.

Experiments were performed within the Directional Solidification Insert (DSI) of the Device for the study of Critical LIquids and Crystallization (DECLIC) aboard the International Space Station. Homogeneous 3D cylindrical samples in a classical Bridgman setup was processed with various pulling velocities V and temperature gradients G. The transparent succinonitrile (SCN)-0.24wt% camphor alloy was the sample material and it permitted in situ optical imaging of the solid/liquid interface. Experiments were typically initiated from a single crystal growing along the temperature gradient direction. The alloy solidified within a cylindrical crucible with an inner diameter of 10mm. The solid/liquid interface was located within a stable and well-controlled temperature gradient. The crucible was pulled through an axial adiabatic zone, allowing the interface to grow up to 100 mm in length at a controlled velocity. While independently controlling V and G experienced by the interface, in situ evolution of the solid/liquid interface morphology was imaged and analyzed. 3D phase-field simulations were specifically developed to identify ranges of primary spacings for the formation of the classical

From the technological viewpoint, the importance of cellular and dendritic microstructures is quite clear since these structures are exhibited in all important commercial solidification techniques. The proposed project will for the first time provide benchmark data for the dynamical evolution of three-dimensional cellular and dendritic patterns that will enable precise modeling of complex commercial processing technologies to give reliable products. The development of a reliable model will allow industries to design new materials and processing conditions that will have a significant impact on the economy in the US, since casting and welding industries are several billion dollars industries. In addition, the fundamental knowledge of pattern formation will allow the development of nano-scale patterns in polymers and electronic materials that will have significant impact on the development of high technology and advanced materials.

The objective of the ACE-TR (Ellipsoid) experiment was to image and document the self-assembly of complex 3D structures formed from small elliptical colloidal particles suspended in a fluid. Temperature gradients were varied with the objective to explore the effect of thermophoresis on colloidal crystallization. The goal was to crystallize a metastable colloidal liquid to study how the orientation and periodicity in particle arrangement evolves in different regions of the phase diagram of elliptical colloidal particles. The objective was to understand the effects of gravity on colloidal self-assembly, test predictions of current theories for soft materials, and develop novel techniques that can be applied to combine materials with different densities in additive manufacturing. The expected outcome has the potential to make novel colloidal materials in a Low-Earth orbit and return them to Earth.

Despite the fundamental and technological importance, the understanding of colloidal crystallization is still elusive. This investigation hypothesizes that there is interrelation between processes driving orientation and periodicity in particle arrangement. Comparing the outcome of the ACE-T11 (Hard Spheres) and ACE-TR (Ellipsoids) experiments should help elucidate this interrelation. This will enable a better understanding at the particle level of how a disordered arrangement of elliptical particles self-organizes into a 3D ordered structure.

ACE-TR will view collections of temperature-controlled, fluorescent-core micron-sized colloidal particles. It uses two different sets of ellipsoids, each in their own sample cells. These have aspect ratios of either 1x2.8 or 1x4.5 microns. The particles are small enough that 50 of them could be placed end to end across the width of a fine human hair; yet big enough that the particles and the structures they form can be photographed with visible light of a confocal microscope. The observations will be done using a 3D confocal microscope at the particle level for sufficiently high particle concentrations; in some samples, we will attempt to control the desired concentration by applying a temperature gradient, to see if the particle number density will adjust itself as a function of temperature throughout the sample cell. ImageJ software and internally developed MATLAB functions and scripts were used for processing and quantification of images collected.

ACE-TR reveals several fundamental and practical aspects of soft matter science with potential applications on Earth. Self-assembly processes are crucial to making functional materials and devices from small particles. Improved design and assembly of structures fabricated in microgravity may have use in a variety of fields from medicine to opto-electronics on Earth. Ultimately, the ability to design and build functional structures based on colloids will allow new devices for chemical energy, communication, and photonics, including photonic materials to control and manipulate light. The rapidly growing fields of 3D printing and additive manufacturing rely on the assembly and sintering of particle aggregates and the preparation of high-density slurries and pastes of different colloidal materials and with different rheological and mechanical properties. These ellipsoids may behave like liquid crystals when they self-assemble and their possible defects (hedgehogs) may also be visible.

The objective of this project is to understand phase selection in structural alloys and to investigate the effects of convection on time-dependent nucleation phenomena during rapid solidification from the melt. The ELFSTONE investigation involves a collaboration with the European Space Agency's (ESA) Thermolab Experiment which focuses on thermophysical properties data measurement of industrial alloys in the liquid phase as a function of temperature. The property values obtained are used to increase the accuracy of numerical modeling of casting and solidification processes of metal alloys. For access to data relating to the Thermolab Experiment, please consult ESA's HRE Data Archive (hreda.esac.esa.int)

The experimental hypothesis was that melt convection would significantly decrease the nucleation kinetics for transformation of metastable ferrite to stable austenite in ferrous structural steel alloys. The was successfully observed.

The samples are processed in the Electromagnetic Levitator (ISS-EML), a facility that has been operational since 2015 and is located in the Columbus module. The investigation is part of Sample Batch 1 - the first of six proposed 18-sample multi-user cartridges uploaded to the ISS. For the ELFSTONE Sample #09, a ternary FeCrNi analog steel sample, a process cycle is defined as (1) the melting of the sample, (2) the gathering of science data, and (3) the subsequent undercooling and rapid solidification of the sample. The next cycle starts with the re-melting of the sample. In any particular cycle, stirring may be induced at different levels to study the effect of convection on rapid solidification behavior. After all cycles are complete, final microstructure is preserved for return to earth.

The value of this research is that the results have application to the design of industrial welding, spray forming, and casting operations for a commercially important class of structural materials. In addition, this research addresses fundamental issues relating to rapid solidification behavior, metastable phase selection, and analysis of the processes governing microstructural evolution. Experiments focus on the use of convection as a processing control parameter.

docs.title: Microheater Array Boiling Experiment
passages: PSI-81 · MABE — Microheater Array Boiling Experiment
PSI-81 · MABE — Microheater Array Boiling Experiment
PSI-81 · MABE — Microheater Array Boiling Experiment
PSI-81 · MABE — Microheater Array Boiling Experiment
Keywords: MABE · microscale heater array · boiling · bubble dynamics

1. To characterize the boiling curve in a very low g-jitter environment: The experiment aims to determine the boiling curve in a microgravity environment with minimal gravitational disturbances (g-jitter). This objective is driven by the understanding that g-jitter can significantly influence bubble dynamics and, consequently, the heat transfer process. By minimizing g-jitter, the researchers hope to obtain a clearer picture of boiling behavior in a true microgravity environment.

2. To understand the parameters governing the size of the primary bubble and develop a predictive model for it: A key objective is to identify the factors that determine the size of the primary bubble in microgravity. These parameters could include heater size, nucleation site density, subcooling, gravity level, fluid properties, superheated layer thickness, wall superheat, and surface tension. By understanding these parameters, the researchers aim to develop a model that can accurately predict the primary bubble size under different conditions.

3. To investigate the mechanism of critical heat flux (CHF) in microgravity and its relationship to the primary bubble: The research aims to elucidate how CHF occurs in microgravity and to determine its relationship to the size and behavior of the primary bubble. CHF is a critical parameter in boiling, representing the maximum heat flux that can be transferred from a surface before a transition to film boiling occurs. Understanding the factors influencing CHF in microgravity is essential for the safe and efficient operation of space-based thermal systems.

4. To determine the effect of heater size on the formation of the primary bubble and its impact on the boiling curve: MABE investigates the influence of heater size on boiling behavior. Two different heater array sizes are used, allowing the researchers to compare how heater size affects the formation of the primary bubble, the occurrence of dryout, and the shape of the boiling curve in microgravity.

This study will test three central hypotheses: (1) Bubble coalescence dominates heat transfer in microgravity, creating a large primary bubble that induces local dryout; (2) A transition between buoyancy-dominated and surface-tension-dominated boiling regimes occurs depending on the interplay between the heater size and the gravitational acceleration; (3) Heat transfer in the surface-tension-dominated regime shows minimal dependence on gravitational acceleration.

MABE utilizes a multi-pronged approach to achieve its research objectives. The experiment combines a carefully designed experimental setup with a comprehensive data analysis strategy. Here's a breakdown of the key elements of the investigation approach:
Microscale heater array: The experiment utilizes an array of 96 individually controlled platinum resistance heaters deposited on a quartz substrate.
Constant temperature control: Each heater is maintained at a constant temperature, allowing for accurate quantification of substrate heat conduction and reducing the risk of heater burnout.
Variable experimental conditions: The experiment manipulates key parameters such as bulk liquid subcooling, pressure, and heater size to study their influence on boiling.

Multiple gravity levels: The experiment is designed to allow data acquisition in Earth gravity, lunar gravity, Martian gravity, and microgravity, enabling a comprehensive comparison of boiling behavior across different gravitational environments.
High-speed video imaging: A high-speed digital camera captures images of the boiling process beneath the heater array, providing valuable insights into bubble dynamics.
Interferometry: The experiment employs interferometry to measure temperature profiles around the vapor bubble, providing additional data for analysis.
Data Acquisition: Data is collected at a high frequency, capturing the instantaneous power dissipated by each heater, bulk fluid temperature, pressure, and acceleration.
Data Processing: Raw data is converted into engineering units, synchronized, and analyzed to generate boiling curves, heat transfer maps, and other relevant data visualizations.

Correlation with video and interferometry data: The heat transfer data is correlated with visual observations from the high-speed video and interferometry data to gain a deeper understanding of bubble behavior and heat transfer mechanisms.
Analytical and Numerical Modeling: The experiment employs analytical and numerical models to simulate the boiling process and validate the experimental findings.

Preliminary Engineering Model: A preliminary engineering model of the experiment is developed and tested on the KC-135 aircraft, providing essential validation of the design and data acquisition procedures.
Calibration and Validation: The heater array is calibrated on the ground and recalibrated in flight to ensure accurate measurements.
This investigation approach combines a sophisticated experimental setup with rigorous data analysis and modeling to provide a comprehensive understanding of boiling in microgravity.

In microgravity, a bubble can cover an entire heater array instead of just a small area, resulting in burnout of components if local hot spots are present. The increased spatial resolution of these measurements will enable the extent of the dry spot to be measured along with the heat transfer from the liquid surrounding the dry spot. This technique can be applied to other areas including spray cooling, turbulence measurements and flow boiling. The proposed research has shown that transient conduction is the dominant heat transfer mechanism in boiling of refrigerants-like fluids. This research will provide insight into creating more efficient cooling systems on Earth.

1. To use microbial strains that are relevant to human spaceflight, and nosocomial infections that have also occurred in spaceflight, and substrata materials that are relevant to (i) spacecraft structures and surfaces, (ii) life support systems, (iii) space biology research hardware, and (iv) medical instrumentation. We are meeting this objective by the use of the same fungal strain that was isolated from a bio-damaged Mir window (Penicillium rubens), and an uropathogenic bacterial strain (Pseudomonas aeruginosa). 2. To culture the selected microbial strains in a way that enables biofilm formation, during an up- to-6-month experiment. To achieve this goal, we used BioServe’s already spaceflight- proven hardware and conducted preliminary testing during the first year of the experiment. 3. To quantify potential changes on biofilm mass, thickness, and overall morphology (including the formation of the “column-and-canopy structures) on the spaceflight cultures with respect to matched ground controls. This was achieved by acquiring post-flight (samples fixed in paraformaldehyde) morphological data through confocal laser scanning microscopy. 4. To elucidate the molecular mechanisms behin

It is hypothesized that, in comparison to matched ground controls: a) Biofilm mass and thickness in microgravity will be increased for all bacterial and fungal species, growth medium, and substratum material; b) Gene expression will vary as a function of growth medium, substratum material, and gravitational regime; c) A systematic increase in expression of the genes that confer microorganisms with oxidative, acidity, and antimicrobial resistance will be observed in space (becoming more pronounced with time in space); and d) The formation of the “column-and- canopy” bacterial biofilm architecture and the material/microorganism interaction mechanisms in space will vary from one microbial species and material to the other, and will be associated with the differential expression of specific genes.

The Space Biofilms project, performed at the International Space Station, contributes to the understanding of microbial communities in space by characterizing the morphology and gene expression of bacterial and fungal biofilms formed in microgravity with respect to ground controls. The project has two big branches, the bacterial and the fungal side. Pseudomonas aeruginosa was used as model organism for the bacterial side and both morphology and transcriptomic (selected samples) studies were performed with bacterial samples, while Penicillium rubens was used as model organism for the fungal side and a morphology study was performed for fungal samples. Bacterial biofilm formation was characterized at one, two, and three days of incubation (37°C) over six different materials: stainless steel 316, passivated stainless steel 316, a lubricant impregnated surface (LIS), catheter grade silicone with and without a linear microtopography, and cellulose membrane. Fungal biofilm formation (mold) was characterized at 10, 15, and 20 days of incubation (25°C) over seven different materials: stainless steel 316, aluminum alloy (Al6061), titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V), quartz, catheter grade silicone,

This project is relevant to the space program and the “Biophysics – Biomaterials” emphasis of this NRA as it investigates biofilm formation (which can increase the risk of astronaut infection and equipment failure) on spacecraft-relevant materials. This work is relevant to the Space Biology Program and the Human Research Roadmap as it utilizes human pathology-associated bacterial species (uropathogenic Pseudomonas aeruginosa), growth media (e.g. modified artificial urine media), and materials (e.g. silicone from catheters).The knowledge produced may help address Gaps Micro-01, -02, -03, and -04 by characterizing bacterial and fungal responses to spaceflight, by interrogating the expression of genes associated with drug resistance, and by elucidating the governing mechanisms behind the observed phenomena. Furthermore, due to our proposed approach, the knowledge derived from this project may be translatable to biofilm-associated illnesses on Earth.

Keywords: EHD · electric conduction · electric fields · boiling · Reduced Gravity · Electrodrodynamics · dielectrophoresis · critical heat flux · heat transfer · Presence of Gravity

a-Provide fundamental understanding of the combined electrically driven (based on EHD conduction phenomenon) liquid film flow and dielectroporetic vapor extraction mechanism in the presence of phase change (liquid to vapor) in the absence of gravity.

b-Provide a phenomenological foundation for the future development of electric field based two phase thermal management systems, leveraging EHD engineering advantages to develop systems of arbitrary mass flow requirements and geometries.

Boiling is not acceptable in the absence of gravity unless the generated vapor bubbles can be expelled from the boiling surface and fresh liquid can be pumped onto the hot surface through some mechanism. EHD conduction pumping has the capability of pumping thin liquid films toward the heat source where the boiling takes place, with sufficient inertia to begin expelling bubbles from the heated surface at low heat fluxes. Furthermore, applying an EHD Dielectrophoretic (DEP) extraction force near the boiling surface guarantees the repulsion of vapor bubbles away from the heated surface even at high heat fluxes. Finally, the combined EHD driven liquid film flow boiling and DEP extraction force are expected to sustain and enhance the critical heat flux in the absence of gravity. Combining EHD conduction and DEP effects is therefore critical to the success of the ISS experiment.

As vapor bubbles cover the surface and grow or coalesce, the modes of heat transfer will be limited to conduction and possibly radiation. To avoid this and to enable boiling to take place, EHD-driven liquid film will be fed from the condenser section towards the heater. The inertia of liquid film flow along with DEP extraction force will repel vapor bubbles that have formed on the heater surface. In order to study the competing effects of flow inertia/DEP extraction force vs. bubble behavior in zero gravity, one needs to understand EHD generated liquid film flow and the DEP mechanism. The flow inertia is a function of applied EHD potential, electrode design, liquid film thickness and working fluid properties. The DEP extraction force is also a function of its corresponding electrode design, the spacing between its electrode and heated surface, and the applied potential for a given working fluid. Thus, the controlling parameters for this study are applied EHD conduction pumping potential, applied DEP potential, heat flux, and liquid film height for the selected working fluid and electrode designs. This multi-physics proposal will provide basic scientific understanding about competing physical phenomena of flow inertia and bubble dynamics in electrically driven liquid film flow boiling in the presence of electric bubble extraction force (i.e., dielectrophoretic force) in microgravity. Keywords: dendritic growth · Ivantsov solution · Dendrite Tip Velocity · Interfacial Energy · microgravity · Buoyancy-induced Convection · Dendrite Radius of Curvature · Succinonitrile

The primary objective of the microgravity dendritic growth experiment was to measure definitively the kinetics and morphology of dendritic growth, and to account for the effects of natural convection. The experimental objective was to use a single,clearly defined experimental parameter, namely, the supercooling, to fully determine the resulting steady-state dendritic growth velocity, V, and tip radius R. Designated the IDGE, the first flight, manifested on the second United States Microgravity Payload (USMP-2) mission, was launched and operated on the STS-62 on March 4-18, 1994. This IDGE investigation met the objective of acquiring accurate dendritic growth speed and morphology data under diffusion-controlled conditions, while greatly reducing buoyancy-induced convective heat transport through the reduction of gravity. The microgravity environment broadened this range of supercooling and permitted for the first time a critical assessment of both the heat transport theory and the interfacial kinetics behavior.

The hypothesis of this investigation is that as a function of the supercooling there exists an explicit dendritic dynamic operating state defined by dendritic tip velocity, V and the dendrite tip paraboloidal radius of curvature, R. The Peclet number obtained from the Ivantsov solution for each specified supercooling yielded an infinite number of solutions for V and R. Therefore it is hypothesized that a second independent equation or length scale exists, which, when combined with the Ivantsov diffusion solution, will mathematically select the observed unique dynamic operating state. Two of the candidates for the additional crystal growth physics that could provide the second crucial equation are the effects from the solid-melt interfacial energy, the influence of temperature fluctuations in the melt, or both.

The approach was to observe and image dendritic growth as a function of undercooling such that dendritic tip velocities and radii could both be accurately measured and used as a critical test of theory. Succinonitrile (SCN), transparent when molten, was used as a model metal analog system for studying dendritic growth since it solidifies like the body centered cubic (BCC) ferrous metal alloys, i.e., with an atomically ''rough'' solid-liquid interface. In addition, SCN displays convenient properties for solidification experiments, such as a low melting temperature (58.08 °C), optical transparency, and the potential for accurate characterization of its thermophysical properties. Dendritic growth is initiated inside the experimental chamber by energizing thermoelectric coolers attached to one end a thin capillary injector tube called the stinger. The other end of the stinger, where the dendrite emerges in the center of the chamber, is notched, much like the tip of a fountain pen. This helps isolate the leading dendrite and reduces the time needed until the leading dendrite is isothermal and has achieved steady state. The IDGE flight experiment was divided into 60 operational cycles. T

The size, shape, spacing, and orientation of the dendrites in cast metal alloys have a major effect on the strength, ductility and toughness. Nearly all cast-metal alloys used in everyday products, such as automobiles and airplanes, are composed of dendritic microstructures. Metallurgists have long sought to predict and control alloy microstructures. The development of automated, cost effective manufacturing techniques ultimately depends on the precision with which the problem in non-equilibrium pattern formation can be solved. In principle, the intent is to incorporate fundamental understanding of microstructures into computer codes that simultaneously help design materials with made to order properties and optimize their manufacturability and performance. Dendritic growth experiments conducted in the microgravity environment can provide benchmark data to validate such predictive models.

The main objective of the DSI-R investigation was to quantitatively establish the fundamental physics controlling the spatiotemporal organization of the secondary sidebranch structure and its interaction with the array structure of primary branches under directional solidification conditions. This investigation particularly focused on the origin of sidebranches that occur when columnar solidification patterns transform from cellular to dendritic as a function of thermal gradient and solidification velocity and study the potential for the formation of an intermediate multiplet pattern. The dynamics and stability of cellular and dendritic growth patterns, and the relationship between the tip geometry and growth pattern were also to be investigated as well. This intent of this investigation was to directly address outstanding issues that remain open in the understanding of complex dendritic microstructures.
Bridgman solidification of transparent binary alloys in a diffusion controlled growth regime can yield benchmark data required for establishing the detailed dynamics of interface pattern selection.

The ''SPAtiotemporal evolution of three-dimensional DEndritic array Structures'' (SPADES) investigation conducted during the reflight of the Directional Solidification Insert (DSI-R) campaign targeted the columnar dendritic growth regime to quantitatively establish the fundamental physics controlling the spatiotemporal organization of the secondary sidebranch structure and its interaction with the array structure of primary branches under directional solidification conditions.
SPADES focused on the origin of sidebranches that occur when columnar solidification patterns transform from cellular to dendritic as a function of thermal gradient and solidification velocity.

The “Effects of Curvature and Unsteady Dynamics on Alloy Solidification Patterns” (CUSP) investigation extended the DSIP and SPADES project into a new direction that addressed the critical effects of the macroscopic curvature of the solidification front and the unsteady dynamics that occurs in response to changes of growth conditions or that is associated with side-branching.

A weak macroscopic interface curvature can have a major effect on both the array pattern evolution and grain structure. The convex and concave interfaces lead to a continuous increase and decrease of the average primary spacing, respectively, and it only attains a stationary value for a flat interface.

The DSI-R investigation utilized a Bridgman type furnace and an experimental cartridge containing the organic transparent alloy of succinonitrile (SCN) - camphor. The nominal concentration was 0.46 wt% camphor. A single crystalline solid seed with a 100 direction parallel to the pulling axial direction is kept unmelted during all experiments. Solidification is performed by pulling the experimental cartridge containing the alloy inside a thermal gradient G at a pulling rate V. The G and V were the primary variable for each experimental run. Images obtained by the direct axial observation, providing top-view interface images, and transverse observations, providing side-view interface images, were analyzed.

By providing a reduced gravity environment where fluid convection is suppressed, space enables the direct experimental observation of the solid-liquid interface dynamics during the solidification process under long-duration and purely diffusive conditions. The acquired benchmark data will make it uniquely possible to critically test computational models of alloy microstructures by quantitative comparisons of modeling predictions and experimental observations, thereby contributing to the development of Integrated Computational Materials and Engineering (ICME) tools for both space and earth applications. Those tools are expected to “shorten development time, optimize designs and reduce costs relative to more traditional strategies involving building prototypes, testing and redesigning philosophies. In addition, understanding alloy solidification in the microgravity environment of space is important to improve in-space processing (manufacturing, joining, and welding) of structural materials that will be used for future space exploration.

Keywords: Microgravity Crystallization · protein structure · Crystal samples · synchrotron radiation · biophysical analysis

The primary objective of this investigation was to understand why protein crystallization experiments in microgravity have generated unexpectedly low or high numbers of crystals. Each outcome may cause experiments designed to obtain a small number of well-separated crystals to fail.

The objective of the proposed investigations is to explore the effects of a hitherto unstudied factor for the nucleation of protein crystals: solution shear flow. Besides providing a novel tool for nucleation control for protein crystallization experiments, the correlation between solution flows and protein crystal nucleation, to be tested in the proposed investigation, will shed light on one of the major mysteries of current space biophysics: the finding that in many cases the number of crystals nucleated in microgravity was greater or smaller than those nucleated on earth.
Hypothesis: The behavior of dense liquid clusters at different rates of convection will have a profound effect on crystal growth.

The main hypothesis underlying the proposed investigations consists of two parts: 1. The existence of nucleation precursors and the correlation between their properties and the nucleation rate can be used to control protein crystal nucleation via solution flow. 2. Enhancement or suppression of nucleation via solution flow, i.e., independently of solution supersaturation, can be used to achieve higher perfection of the grown crystals. 3. A very small fraction of the protein exists in a dense liquid phase in the form of Brownian particles, each a cluster of roughly 105 protein molecules undergoing liquid-like dynamics. 4. Crystal nucleation occurs when a small, ordered domain forms within the highly concentrated liquid-state environment of one of these particles.

Three cassettes containing five capillaries each were loaded with one of three proteins; (1) Lysozyme, (2) p53, and (3) hnRNPA-LC. The observation of these protein clusters were observed with a newly developed technique, called differential dynamic microscopy (DDM). DDM improves a recent method used to study and quantify the dynamics of sub-micrometer particles in solutions from fluctuations in intensity in optical micrographs. All samples were frozen to a temperature of -80C before flight to the ISS. The proteins were thawed and observed over several weeks in the ISS LMM module where they were filmed and photographed. Sample details and experimental parameters are summarized in LMMBio2_Experimental Table in the science document section.

These images provide data that help scientists and engineers understand the forces that control organization and dynamics of matter at microscopic scales. The organization and movement of matter on the microscopic level profoundly affects the macroscopic world and understanding such processes contributes to development of more efficient materials and machines for application on Earth.

The size, shape, spacing, and orientation of the dendrites in cast metal alloys have a major effect on the strength, ductility and toughness. Nearly all cast-metal alloys used in everyday products, such as automobiles and airplanes, are composed of dendritic microstructures. Metallurgists have long sought to predict and control alloy microstructures. The development of automated, cost effective manufacturing techniques ultimately depends on the precision with which the problem in non-equilibrium pattern formation can be solved. The objective of the proposed investigation is to better understand the columnar-to-equiaxed grain structure transition (CET) in solidification of metal alloys. By performing solidification experiments both on earth and in a microgravity environment, the effects of gravity-driven melt convection and sedimentation/floatation of unattached dendrite fragments and equiaxed crystals on the CET will be examined. The origin of equiaxed grains in non-refined alloys is of particular interest in the proposed experiments. The benchmark data from these experiments can be used to test theoretical models and computer simulations.

The primary hypothesis of this investigation is that fragmentation of columnar dendrites can lead to a CET in non-grain-refined alloys. The secondary dendrite arms that detach from the primary columnar trunks are a potent source of new (equiaxed) grains. However, for a CET to occur the growth of the primary columnar trunks must be blocked by equiaxed grains. This can only be accomplished if the secondary dendrite fragments are transported to the columnar front, rather than remain between the primary columnar trunks. Due to natural convection of the melt and sedimentation or floatation of the fragments, such transport can be expected to readily occur in the gravitational field of earth. In the absence of gravity, it is not clear if fragmentation alone, without fragment transport, is sufficient to cause a CET.

Experiments were conducted in the Solidification Using a Baffle in Sealed Ampoules (SUBSA) furnace to investigate the CET for stationary samples without an imposed temperature gradient. Most experiments with aluminum-copper (Al-Cu) alloys, namely, Al-4wt%Cu, Al-10wt%Cu and Al-18wt%Cu alloys. The reason is that Al-Cu alloys are better suited for the duplicate ground-based experiments. If solidified upward (low temperature at the bottom, high at the top), thermosolutal natural convection of the melt will generally be minimized. The sedimentation or floatation of dendrite fragments and small equiaxed grains can be controlled by the solute concentration. For smaller solute concentrations, the solid is heavier than the melt and will sediment, while for higher solute concentrations the solid is lighter and will float. Hence, dendrite fragments and equiaxed grains in the Al-18wt%Cu alloy will float upwards ahead of the columnar front, and a CET can be expected. On the other hand, for the Al-4wt%Cu alloy, the fragments will sediment and remain between the primary columnar trunks, and a CET may not occur. For Al-10wt%Cu alloys, the solid is approximately neutrally buoyant in the melt. An ad

The CET refers to the transition between the elongated grains in the outer portions of a casting and the more rounded grains in the center. Understanding this transition is fundamental to determining what type of grain structure forms in castings of most metal alloys (steel, aluminum, copper, etc.). Often, a fully equiaxed structure is preferred, but the fully columnar structures of many turbine blades are an important exception. In addition to its high practical significance, the CET represents a “holy grail” in the area of modeling and simulation of casting. This is because in order to realistically predict the CET, almost every physical phenomenon at every length scale must be taken into account simultaneously. This investigation will not only provide an improved understanding of the CET, but also models and computer simulations of the grain structure formation in metal castings that can be used by industry to better industry to better understand and optimize their casting processes.

docs.title: Advanced Colloids Experiment-Temperature 4
passages: Research area: Complex Fluids - Soft Matter
Hardware: Light Microscopy Module (LMM) Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR)
Keywords: Colloidal Glasses · Crystalline Order · Glass Transition · Microgravity

Original Objective: The ACE-T4 experiments were designed to explore the disorder-induced transformation between a crystal and a glass. The experiments introduced disorder by added colloidal dopants into the samples; these dopants introduce structural frustration into the crystals which, in turn, can transform the crystals into disordered solids (polycrystalline) and glasses with novel mechanical properties. The experiments varied the concentration and character of particle dopants in three-dimensional colloidal crystals and employed direct visualization of an evolving crystal microstructure and dynamics in microgravity to derive fundamental insight into the nature of the transition and the glasses formed.

Revised Objective: Before the ACE-T4 experiment on the International Space Station (ISS) was conducted, the master hard disk controlling the Light Microscopy Module (LMM) failed and delayed starting this experiment by many months. This extended delay had a detrimental effect on the samples that resulted in the gelation of the samples before the experiment began. The originally planned experiments were no longer possible due to gelation, but the ACE-T4 experiment based on the changed samples (gels) provided qualitatively different insights into the behavior of 3D colloidal gels over a range of temperatures and temperature gradients. Some effects were visible with LMM and provide an opportunity to study the microstructure, dynamics, and stresses in gels that can lead to microcracks, an important problem that, for example, could affect 3D printer inks.

The ACE-T4 experiments were intended to explore the transformation between a crystal and a glass by varying the density and character of particle dopants in three dimensional colloidal crystals. The original hypothesis stated that ''dopants introduce structural frustration into the crystals which, in turn, can transform the crystals into disordered (polycrystalline) solids and glasses with novel mechanical properties. Direct visualization of the evolving crystal microstructure and dynamics in microgravity will provide fundamental insight into the nature of glasses and into processes such as nucleation and melting.''

The ACE-T4 experiment used confocal microscopy to observe the gels over a range of particle packing-fractions (temperatures), using pure, monodisperse poly(N -isopropylacrylamide) (pNIPA) particles in one sample, and then mixtures of pNIPAM particles with different amounts of particle dopants in five other samples. All of the samples formed gels. There was no crystallization in any sample . The data obtained permits the study of 3D gels with and without dopants as a function of temperature; the temperature changes vary the particle size and thus properties of the gels. In addition to the revised ACE-T4 experiment, ground-based soft matter research was completed and published.

By frustrating their structural order, the transition from ordered (crystal) to disordered (glassy) materials can alter the macroscopic behavior of ordered materials. Moreover, these experiments could also provide fundamental insight into the nature of nucleation, aging, and melting in materials with varying degrees of order. This information could benefit observation and synthesis of new colloidal materials (e.g. g., meta and photonic materials) for many applications ranging from color control to random laser.
