docs.title: Constrained Vapor Bubble
passages: Keywords: Constrained Vapor Bubble (CVB) Experiment · Heat Pipe Technology · Capillary Action · Phase change · Microgravity · Marangoni Flow · Internal Radiation

The immediate macroscopic objectives are to determine the overall stability, the fluid flow characteristics, the average heat transfer coefficient in the evaporator, and the heat conductance of the CVB as a function of vapor volume and heat flow rate. On the microscopic scale, the scientific objective is to evaluate the local details of the Kelvin-Clapeyron model of change-of-phase heat transfer under microgravity conditions where the extended Young-Laplace equation predominates.

It is hypothesized that the isothermal equilibrium liquid film shape depends on the gravitational field and the intermolecular force field which changes rapidly in the vicinity of the liquid-vapor and liquid-solid interfaces. This equilibrium shape in a particular gravitational field can be controlled by fixing the container shape, the liquid-substrate system, and the relative volume of the liquid to that of the vapor. It is further hypothesized that the extended Young-Laplace equation can describe this shape over a large range of conditions. Under non-equilibrium conditions resulting from an imposed temperature gradient, fluid flow and change-of-phase heat transfer are a function of further changes in the shape of the liquid volume. It is postulated that these non-equilibrium effects can be analyzed using a Kelvin-Clapeyron transport model that includes the use of the conservation of heat, mass and momentum and the extended Young-Laplace equation.

The CVB-1 investigation used a variety of methods to study the behavior of the constrained vapor bubble (CVB) in a microgravity environment. This approach involved conducting experiments, creating mathematical models, and using insights from past CVB experiments to analyze the findings after the flight.

1. Experimental Design and Testing: -Customized CVB Cells: Five CVB cells were fabricated from quartz. Each cell featured a square cross-section (3 x 3 mm) and varying lengths to achieve specific liquid-to-vapor volume ratios. One cell was a ''dry'' cell, evacuated to 5 torr, to establish baseline thermal behavior. The remaining four cells were filled with either pentane (a completely wetting fluid) or ethanol (a partially wetting fluid) before launch. Three cells utilized pentane at different volume ratios, while one was intended for ethanol. -Controlled Thermal Environment: The CVB cells were integrated into a system that allowed for precise control of heat input at the evaporator end and heat rejection at the condenser end. The system maintained a stable and uniform thermal environment for the cells. -Microgravity Environment: The CVB experiments were conducted on the International Space Station (ISS) to provide the necessary microgravity conditions.

2. Data Acquisition: -Macroscopic Measurements: Throughout the experiment, macroscopic data were recorded, including temperature profiles along the cell, vapor pressure, heat input and rejection rates, and visual observations of the vapor bubble. These observations were used to assess the overall performance and stability of the CVB system. -Microscopic Measurements: The investigation utilized an Image Analyzing Interferometer (IAI) to acquire detailed, microscopic measurements of the liquid film profile. These measurements included curvature profiles, film thickness profiles, and adsorbed film thickness. These data were crucial for understanding the local transport processes within the CVB. -Acceleration Measurements: The system monitored residual accelerations to assess their potential impact on the CVB's stability and behavior. Time Correlation: All acquired data were meticulously time-correlated to ensure accurate analysis and interpretation.
Extended Young-Laplace Equation: This equation, incorporating both capillary and van der Waals forces, was employed to model the equilibrium shape of the liquid-vapor interface.

Kelvin-Clapeyron Transport Model: This model was used to analyze the non-equilibrium behavior of the CVB. It incorporated conservation equations for mass, momentum, and energy, along with the extended Young-Laplace equation. The model was considered for refinement to account for internal radiative heat transfer, observed in previous experiments. -Numerical Modeling: Two- and three-dimensional numerical thermal modeling were considered to evaluate and refine the Kelvin-Clapeyron model, particularly to capture the complex interplay between capillary and Marangoni convection. -Internal Heat Analysis: Temperature data were analyzed to quantify the contributions of conduction, external radiation, and internal radiation to the overall heat transfer within the CVB system. This analysis built upon previous ground-based studies and included a detailed examination of the role of Marangoni convection.

4. Comparison with Ground-Based Studies: -Equilibrium Studies: The microgravity equilibrium data, including film thickness and curvature profiles, were compared with ground-based measurements to confirm the validity of the extended Young-Laplace equation under these conditions. -Non-Equilibrium Studies: Comparison of microgravity non-equilibrium data with results from ground-based studies illuminated the influence of gravity on CVB behavior. Specifically, this comparison focused on the differences in flow field symmetry and the magnitude of heat transfer.

5. Stability Analysis: -Macroscopic Stability: The investigation evaluated the overall stability of the CVB system, considering the occurrence of dryout, oscillations, and cavitation, as a function of heat flux, liquid-to-vapor volume ratio, and working fluid. -Microscopic Stability: A stability analysis was performed, leveraging experimental observations and mathematical modeling, to understand the conditions and mechanisms that lead to instability within the thin liquid film.

6. Post-Flight Analysis: -Reflectivity and Image Data: Detailed analysis of the raw reflectivity and image data was conducted to extract information about the adsorbed film thickness and its influence on CVB behavior.

CVB has performed ground-based studies in a thermal vacuum chamber to determine the efficiency of the heater and cooler configuration. Large thermal response times that have been experimentally observed in space-based experiments cannot be obtained from these ground-based studies. Space-based experimentation is the only method available to ascertain internal low-gravity fluid mechanics within a heat pipe. The project aims to achieve an improved understanding of microscale heat transfer, improved designs for wickless heat pipes, and an increased efficiency in heat transfer devices for cooling critical components. Targeted users are existing microelectronics industry and perhaps military applications. New designs should be able to be developed several months following the analysis and presentation of the results from the experiment.

passages: PSI-4 · FBCE FBM — Flow Boiling and Condensation Experiment Flow Boiling Module

Keywords: Flow boiling · Two-phase Flow · flow boiling pressure drop · FBCE FBM · Density Wave Oscillations · Pressure Drop Oscillations · Heat transfer

The proposed research aims to develop an integrated two-phase flow boiling/condensation facility for the International Space Station (ISS) to serve as a primary platform for obtaining two-phase flow and heat transfer data in microgravity. By comparing the microgravity data against those obtained in Earth’s gravity, it will be possible to ascertain the influence of body force on two-phase transport phenomena in pursuit of mechanistic models as well as correlations, and to help determine the minimum flow criteria to ensure gravity independent flow boiling and condensation. This research is a joint effort between the Purdue University Boiling and Two-Phase Flow Laboratory (PU-BTPFL) and the NASA Glenn Research Center. Personnel from the two organizations combine extensive experience in research and development of both flow boiling and condensation systems, and in conducting microgravity experiments.

The objectives of the Flow Boiling and the Flow Condensation Experiment (FBCE) in the long duration microgravity environment of the ISS are to: 1. Develop experimentally validated, mechanistic model for microgravity flow boiling critical heat flux (CHF) and dimensionless criteria to predict minimum flow velocity required to ensure gravity independent CHF. 2. Develop experimentally validated, mechanistic model for microgravity annular condensation and dimensionless criteria to predict minimum flow velocity required to ensure gravity independent annular condensation. Also, develop correlations for other condensation regimes in microgravity. 3. Obtain flow boiling data (heat flux, flow visualization, the wall temperature difference) in long duration microgravity environments for a well characterized heating surface as functions of liquid inlet mass velocity and subcooling. 4. Obtain flow condensation data (heat flux, flow visualization, the wall temperature difference) in long duration microgravity environments for a well-characterized condensing surface as functions of inlet quality and flow rate of condensing vapor. Specific tasks for the study will be as follows.

In literature spanning many decades, body force in terrestrial gravity is identified as having a profound influence on two-phase transport behavior. This behavior is drastically altered In the absence of gravity, wherein flow fluid and heat transfer are dictated by flow inertia and surface tension. This implies predictive tools from terrestrial gravity studies are inapplicable for design of NASA's reduced gravity systems. This limitation points to a need for performing two-phase flow and heat transfer experiments on board the ISS as basis for formulating relevant reduced gravity predictive tools.

The approach used in this project is to perform the following sequential series of tasks: 1. Provide detailed design and instrumentation requirements for the Flow Boiling Module (FBM). 2. Provide design and instrumentation requirements for the entire flow loop. 3. Generate test matrix for operating conditions of the study. 4. Perform initial validation tests in both terrestrial gravity and parabolic flight. 5. Perform tests on board the ISS. 6. Based on both the ISS and terrestrial data, develop a series of predictive tools, including empirical correlations as well as theoretical, computational, and machine learning models.

The proposed research will lay the foundation for development of advanced high power to weight ratio thermal management systems for NASA's future space vehicles and planetary bases. Purdue University research has also shown tremendous value in findings from this projects to numerous other applications including ultra-fast charging of electric vehicles, fusion reactors, hydrogen storage, avionics, high-Mach turbine engines, and advanced electronics in laser, microwave, and radar systems.
